Linux prints `%016lx`, so today this is theoretical; rejecting a mask that is not 16 lowercase hex digits would close it.
- The three-arm design does work as its comment claims: in the mutation run below, the `yes` arm passed while only the fallback arm failed, so the reader was demonstrably discriminating and not stuck on one answer.

**5. Comment accuracy.** The SIGWINCH parts of `sst.c:684-692` and `osx.c:59-60` are accurate, including the scope — "a resize no longer reaches here" holds for all three fallback routes, since the other two return before `initscr()`, and there is no path where a *successful* curses session hands the classic readers back (the only `tui_shutdown()` calls are `sst.c:534`, immediately before the farewell, and `sst.c:723`, on the way out of `readinput()`). Nothing material — the new case covers the changed behaviour, and I confirmed independently that it can fail. Two smaller notes:

- `sigwinch_caught()` takes `pgrep -P "$shell" | head -1` without checking the process is `sst`. If a game died just after printing `COMMAND>`, the first child would be `sleep 30`, whose mask is `0` — and the two arms that expect `no` would pass on it. `wait_for 'COMMAND'` makes that unlikely; matching `/proc/$gp/cmdline` against `sst` would make it impossible.

All from `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek`, worktree at `main` (`0531ec2`) plus the four unstaged files; nothing committed on `fix/restore-sigwinch`.

1. `cmake --preset ci-debug && cmake --build --preset ci-debug` — clean, zero warning lines (`-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror -std=gnu17`).
2. `cmake --preset ci-release && cmake --build --preset ci-release` — clean.
3. `ctest --preset ci-debug` — 11/11 passed, 297s. `ctest --preset ci-release` — 11/11 passed, 288s. Logs in `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-scottdensmore-Developer-scottdensmore-super-star-trek/8bd691e1-6038-4f0d-82d9-378514dcc470/scratchpad/ctest-{debug,release}.log`.
4. `shellcheck -s sh tests/tui.sh` — clean; plus the disable-removal experiment on a copy.
5. Piped plain-mode journey and `-t`-with-no-tty journey (`printf 'regular\nshort\nnovice\nxyz\nsrscan\nquit\nn\n' | build/ci-debug/sst`), run in a scratch directory: exit 0, correct fallback notice, farewell printed.

passes the whole file** — measured for both. Neither case pins its
retry any more; they pin the player-facing promise, and the new arms pin

Merged as `0fa9127`. `main` clean, #152 closed.

## Session totals

**Eight issues closed across seven merged PRs:**

| | |
|---|---|
| `3e0c97f` | **#90** — stale columns outside every curses window |
| `4fe5088` | **#125** — `CMakePresets.json` as the one place the build is defined |

| `0531ec2` | **#156** — a comment's claims are answerable too |
| `0fa9127` | **#152** — put SIGWINCH back when the panels are given up |

Plus **#146** closed by cleaning the build trees, and **#122** two-thirds resolved incidentally with the remainder documented on it.

**37 issues open**, ten of them filed this session and all verified against the code before filing.

## The arc

The five TUI changes chained: each fix made the next defect reachable. Fixing the short-terminal band let a reviewer reach the fallback game, which surfaced a resize ending the session, which made "enlarge, finish, play again" ordinary — and that's #154, still open. The last two closed the loop: #150 hardened the symptom, #152 removed the cause.

## What I'd carry forward

The rule I added in #157 caught its own author **one commit later**. I wrote "SIGTSTP and SIGCONT still reach this read" as justification, without measuring it, and the `verifier` measured it false. Four more comment claims failed the same way in that one change. Every fix after that came from running the experiment rather than reasoning from the neighbouring case — and the reviewers started running their own mutation matrices to check mine.

That's the most useful thing this session produced, more than any individual fix: the discipline is now written down where the next session inherits it instead of re-deriving it.

## Next, if you want a pointer

**#153** is a one-line `.gitignore` fix — five minutes including the workflow. **#141** and **#89** remain the best contained player-facing slices. **#158** needs its conflicting measurements settled in a real terminal before it can be fixed, and I'd start there only with a terminal you can drive by hand.

# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it
straight away — while the game is waiting for you to answer, and while
it is waiting for a keystroke at a pause — and both the question you
were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so
long as there is still room for them. Older text that no longer fits
scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.

Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for, they clip rather
than rearrange themselves. A line with more to show than there is room
for ends in `>`, so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small
one, and a heading with no room left is dropped rather than shortened.
A terminal too short for the panels is the panels' problem, not the
conversation's: they lose rows off the bottom, the grid keeping its
numbering for as long as it has rows to number, and the conversation
keeps three rows down to six — two of it and the line the prompt or the
pager sits on. Below six there is not that much left to divide and it
keeps what there is: two rows at five and one at four. So the prompt
stays on screen down to four rows, and down to six a paged command shows
a line of itself before stopping to ask — at five its one line goes to
the blank that `lrscan`, `chart` and `status` open with, though
`srscan`, which has none, still shows a line there, and at four the
pager takes the only row and a paged command shows nothing of itself at
all. Shorter than four the panels have taken the screen: the game still
reads what you type, with nothing on it to say so.

Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the
squeeze went: they redraw from the game state, so they return full of
live readings. The conversation cannot be rebuilt that way — curses
does not reflow it — so whatever scrolled away while the window was
small is gone for good, and an older line that was cut short stays cut
short. Every reading is a command away, though, and none of them costs
anything: `srscan`, `status`, `chart`, `damages`.

The line you are on usually comes back, and it is the one that matters:
a question or a pause the game was part way through writing is written
out again whole once there is room for it, so you are not left typing
into the tail of a prompt. A few prompts finish their line before they
stop to wait; those come back too, with the answer going on the row
below the question — or after it, where the window is down to its last
row.
Only their final line comes back, so a question asked over several
lines returns as the last of them. An answer you had already started
typing usually comes back with its question, on the row below it. You
may get back only one of them. Where the question ended its own line the
two sit on separate rows, so a wrapped answer needs three rows and a
window of one or two — five rows or fewer — cannot hold the pair; a
question that has itself wrapped needs a row more again. The question is
what goes, leaving your own typing with nothing above it to say what it
answers, and on a very wide terminal it is the answer that goes instead,
however tall the window is. Shorter still and only part of whichever
survived is left, and sometimes neither comes back, leaving older
conversation on screen with the game waiting behind it.

When the question and everything you typed are both on screen, carry on
and answer — that is the ordinary case now. When they are not, give the
terminal another row or two first: that usually brings it back with
your typing untouched, which beats retyping it. A very wide terminal is
the exception — more rows will not bring the answer back there, though
making it narrow enough will.

If it does not come back, or the terminal cannot grow, do not just
answer it, and do not press Enter either: whatever you typed is still
in the buffer, and a yes/no question reads the *first* letter, so an
`N` typed after a `y` you cannot see answers yes.
Press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away, and then answer. What
you type lands on whatever the window happens to be showing; the line
it fell on clears when you press Enter, though the characters you
typed stay where they landed.

If the prompt is missing or cut off and you had not started answering
it, press Enter. Nothing waiting behind one commits you to anything
then: a pause moves on, the self-destruct password reads the empty
answer as a refusal and stands the sequence down, and a yes/no
question comes back only as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, without
saying again what it asked — answer `N` there and you are back at the
prompt, free to give the command again.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead, and
stays classic for the rest of the session: the choice is made once at
startup, so enlarging the window afterwards will not bring the panels,
and neither will starting a second game from the play-again prompt.

### Building

The build is CMake, driven through presets:

```sh
cmake --preset debug           # or release
cmake --build --preset debug
./build/debug/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler, CMake 3.21 or newer, and ncurses
(`libncurses-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu; already present on macOS).
`ctest --preset debug` runs the test suite, which includes a full-screen
session driven through a real terminal and needs `tmux` — without it
that one test reports as skipped.

`cmake --list-presets` shows them all. There are four: `debug` and
`release`, and `ci-debug` and `ci-release`, which add `-Werror` and are
exactly what CI runs — so you can reproduce a CI warning locally rather
than discovering it in a pull request.

### Windows

There is no working Windows build at the moment.

The old instructions here were `cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c` from a
Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt. That has not worked for some
time: `tui.c` includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and `sst.c`,
`finish.c` and `osx.c` all call into it, so the full-screen display
cannot simply be left out of the file list either.

Making it work again means stubbing the display out under `#ifdef
WINDOWS` — `tui_init()` returning false, so the game always runs in its
classic scrolling form — and then actually building it on Windows to
find out what else has drifted. Nobody has a toolchain in play to check
that, so rather than leave instructions that fail, this says so.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    name: build-and-test (${{ matrix.os }}, ${{ matrix.preset }})
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      # Preset names rather than build types, because the preset is what
      # this job actually runs. A matrix of build types would have to be
      # mapped back to a preset in three separate steps, which is the
      # kind of restatement CMakePresets.json exists to remove.
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
        preset: [ci-debug, ci-release]

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # tmux gives tests/tui.sh the pty that curses needs. Without it
      # that test reports SKIPPED and the job still goes green, so the
      # only coverage of the full-screen display would quietly be none.
      - name: Install ncurses and tmux
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libncurses-dev tmux

      - name: Install tmux
        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
        env:
          HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE: 1
        run: brew list tmux >/dev/null 2>&1 || brew install tmux

      # Every flag these steps would otherwise spell out lives in
      # CMakePresets.json instead: the build type, -Werror via SST_WERROR,
      # and ctest's --output-on-failure and --no-tests=error. Anyone can
      # now run exactly what CI runs with the same three commands, which
      # was not true while this file was one of five writing the recipe
      # down. Three of those five were identical. Only this file carried
      # SST_WERROR, and the verifier's brief -- the pass that stands
      # between a change and CI -- omitted it where the omission
      # mattered, so the one build meant to predict CI was the one that
      # could not.
      - name: Configure
        run: cmake --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

      - name: Build
        run: cmake --build --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

      - name: Test
        run: ctest --preset ${{ matrix.preset }}

input.command:
gh issue create --title "sst.doc says freeze always creates a '.TRK' file; it does not when the name has a dot" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## What is wrong

`sst.doc:1103-1105` describes `freeze` without qualification:

> A file with the specified <file name> and type '.TRK' is created (if
> necessary) in the current directory, and all pertinent information
> about the game is written to that file.

The code appends the extension only when the name the player typed
contains no dot:

```c
	chew();
	if (strchr(citem, '.') == NULL) {
		strcat(citem, ".trk");
	}
```

`setup.c:51-53`. So `freeze save.dat` writes `save.dat` and no `.TRK`
file is created at all.

## Why it matters

A player who read the manual and typed `freeze save.dat` looks for
`save.dat.TRK`, or for `save.dat` having become a `.TRK` file, and finds
neither described anywhere. The manual is the only place the naming rule
is stated, and it states a rule the game does not follow.

The behaviour itself is self-consistent and is not what this issue asks
to change: `thaw` applies the identical test (`setup.c:94-96`), so
`freeze save.dat` / `thaw save.dat` round-trips correctly. Only the
documentation is wrong.

## How to see it

```sh
cmake --preset debug && cmake --build --preset debug
cd "$(mktemp -d)" && cp /path/to/repo/sst.doc .
/path/to/repo/build/debug/sst
```

Start any game, `freeze save.dat`, then `ls`: `save.dat`, no `.trk`.
Repeat with `freeze save` for the documented shape: `save.trk`.

## Where it was found

Measuring what the game writes for #153 (`.gitignore` coverage of saved
games). The `*.trk` rule landed there does not cover `save.dat`, and its
comment records that; this issue is the manual's side of the same fact,
which #153 did not touch.

## Fixing it

Either wording is defensible and it is a judgment call which:

- Document the rule — say the extension is added when the name has none,
  and that a name with a dot is used as typed. Matches `freeze` and
  `thaw` as they are, and needs no code change.
- Make the code match the manual — always append `.trk`. That changes the
  filename `freeze save.dat` produces, so it would need the same change in
  `thaw` and would not find files saved by earlier versions.

The first is the smaller slice and the one this repo's manual is
otherwise written for; the second is a behaviour change that wants its own
argument. Note the 9-character cap the prompt advertises
(`setup.c:42`) is a separate matter and not part of this.
EOF
)"

## Verdict

**Request changes** — one should-fix, on the sentence you asked me to check (though not the clause you rewrote).

State reviewed: branch `chore/gitignore-trk`, HEAD `0fa9127` (identical to `main`, no commits), one unstaged hunk in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.gitignore` adding a 24-line comment block plus the rule `*.trk`. Nothing staged, nothing untracked (`git status --porcelain` shows only ` M .gitignore`). `git diff main...HEAD` is empty; the whole change is the unstaged hunk.

## Findings

### should-fix — `.gitignore:221-225`, the plaque sentence asserts an unconditional escape the rule contradicts

"The plaque at the end of a game escapes as well" is a universal, and the paragraph it sits in has just defined "escapes" as *not matched by `*.trk`* (`save.dat` "is not", `mysave.tr` "neither is"). A player who answers "File or device name for your plaque:" with `winner.trk` gets a file that `*.trk` matches — I confirmed with `git check-ignore -v`, which reports `.gitignore:228:*.trk` for that name. So the outcome claim is false in exactly the case the rest of the paragraph teaches the reader to look for, and false in the direction that matters: a maintainer told the plaque shows in `git status` and finding it does not.

This is the same species as the three corrected before it — an outcome stated where the mechanism was meant — and the fix removes text rather than adding a fourth category. Something like:

```
# The plaque at the end of a game gets none of that shaping: it goes
# through readinput rather than scan, so it opens the name as typed,
# with neither the nine characters nor the extension applied to it
# (finish.c:422-425).
```

"gets none of that shaping" is true without exception and lets the reader derive both directions, including `winner.trk`. Closes #153.

## The slice

One rule, `*.trk`, and a comment recording what it does and does not
catch.

`freeze` opens the name it was given without qualifying it
(`setup.c:55`), so an ordinary one lands in whatever directory the game
is playing in — and that is the source tree, because AGENTS.md's "Build
and run" runs `./build/debug/sst` from the root and the in-game help
reads `sst.doc` from the current directory (`sst.c:161`). A frozen game,
or the `emexit` that freezes to a fixed `emsave.trk` (`sst.c:356`,
`setup.c:38-39`), left an untracked file in `git status` that could be
committed by accident.

Unanchored, unlike its two neighbours, because the game plays in
whatever directory it was started from and that need not be the root.

## The issue's premise was wrong, and the correction is posted on it

#153 assumed one line covers what the game writes. It does not. Measured
by playing:

| typed | written | caught |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `freeze mygame` | `mygame.trk` | yes |
| `freeze save.trk` | `save.trk` | yes |
| `emexit` | `emsave.trk` | yes |
| `freeze save.dat` | `save.dat` | **no** |
| `freeze mysave.trk` | `mysave.tr` | **no** |

`scan()` lowercases the typed name and keeps its first nine characters
(`sst.c:788`), then `.trk` is appended only if what survives has no dot
(`setup.c:51-53`). The last row is those two interacting: `mysave.trk`
is cut to `mysave.tr`, which still has a dot, so nothing is appended.
The plaque a won game offers escapes as well, taking its name through
`readinput` rather than `scan` (`finish.c:422-425`).

That measurement is [posted on the issue](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/issues/153),
per the workflow's step 3 — the slice is unchanged, since what is worth
ignoring was never the part that was wrong.

## Six rounds, six false statements, all the same shape

The rule line is byte-identical to the first draft. Every round went to
the comment, and every false statement found was a sentence asserting an
**outcome** rather than a mechanism:

1. "names somebody typed" as the dividing line — `freeze mygame` is typed and is caught.
2. "a name where the player supplied the extension" escapes — `freeze save.trk` is caught.
3. the covered list omitted the nine-character truncation — `freeze mysave.trk` → `mysave.tr`.
4. "a saved game you cannot see is one you can commit by accident" — backwards; an *ignored* file is the one `git add -A` will not stage. This inverted this PR's own rationale.
5. "what escapes stays visible in `git status`" — false for `freeze a.out`, caught by `*.out` at `.gitignore:36`.
6. the plaque asserted as an unconditional escape — a typed `winner.trk` is caught.

So nothing outcome-shaped survives. The block states the mechanism and
gives four worked examples as illustrations, not as a taxonomy. Each of
1-3 and 6 was found by `code-review`, 4 and 5 by `verifier`.

## Resolved explicitly rather than fixed

- **`verifier` raised three edge cases** — a digit-leading name rejected outright, `freeze .trk` falling through to the prompt, and `freeze my game` writing `my.trk`. Left out. `code-review` recommended against adding them on the grounds that a fourth list is what produced the false statements above, and I agree. `verifier` corrected my reasoning for omitting the third and it was right: `freeze my game` *is* shaped normally, and the reason to omit it is stronger — the shaping still yields a `.trk`, so the rule catches it and no reader is misled.
- **`code-review` flagged "the plaque at the end of a game"** as locating it more broadly than `finish.c:132-154` allows. Not fixed: the clause says when in a session the thing occurs, not how often, and the mechanism after the colon is what the sentence is for. Put back to the reviewer, which withdrew the finding and added the better reason — the plaque is the one file the rule does *not* catch, so over-locating it makes an uncaught case look more frequent, never an ignored file look visible.

## Filed, not fixed

- **#160** — `sst.doc:1103-1105` promises a `.TRK` file unconditionally; `setup.c:51-53` skips the extension for a dotted name. Two further comments on it record the nine-character truncation and the rejection of a name that does not start with a letter, both undocumented. One fix, so one issue.

All four CI jobs pass, merge state CLEAN. #153 is ready at **[PR #161](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/pull/161)**.

**What shipped** — one line, `*.trk`, plus a comment. `freeze` opens the name it was given without qualifying it, so an ordinary save lands in the directory the game plays in, and that's the source tree.

**The issue's premise was wrong.** #153 assumed one line covers what the game writes. Measured by playing: `freeze save.dat` → `save.dat`, and `freeze mysave.trk` → `mysave.tr` — `scan()` truncates to nine characters *before* `setup.c:51` tests for a dot, so the dot survives and nothing is appended. The plaque escapes too. Posted on the issue; the slice itself didn't change.

**Six review rounds, six false statements, every one the same shape** — a sentence asserting an outcome rather than a mechanism. The worst inverted the change's own rationale ("a saved game you cannot see is one you can commit by accident" — an ignored file is precisely the one `git add -A` won't stage). `code-review` caught four, `verifier` two. The block now states the mechanism and gives four worked examples; nothing outcome-shaped is left. The rule line never changed.

Two findings I resolved rather than fixed, both recorded in the PR body: the three edge cases `verifier` raised (a fourth list is what caused the six failures — and it corrected my reasoning for omitting one, rightly), and the plaque locator, which `code-review` withdrew after I put it back with the argument.

**Filed: #160** — `sst.doc:1103-1105` promises a `.TRK` file unconditionally. Two comments on it add the undocumented nine-character truncation and the rejection of any name not starting with a letter. One fix, so one issue rather than three.

**Verification:** `verifier` PASS with the full battery (11/11 in both `ci-*` presets, clean under `-Werror`); `code-review` approve; `ui-review` skipped — `.gitignore` is not compiled, not read at runtime, and shows a player nothing, a claim both other passes checked against the diff. The commit differs from the approved state only by a whitespace reflow `code-review` wrote itself.

Merge it?

═══ #148 ═══
A pause mid-move repaints the panels with the new quadrant's title over the old grid
## Problem

A pause that falls in the middle of a warp move repaints the panels from
game state that is half updated: the quadrant panel's title and the
status panel's `Position` line already name the **new** quadrant, while
the grid still shows the **old** one's contents.

The panels are the display's claim to be a live reading of where the
ship is. For the length of that pause they are not, and nothing on
screen says so.

## Why

`moving.c` sets the new coordinates before it fills the new quadrant:

```c
123    quadx = (ix+9)/10;
124    quady = (iy+9)/10;
...
128    if (quadx != oldquadx || quady != oldquady) {
129        proutn("\nEntering");
130        cramlc(1, quadx, quady);
...
134    skip(1);
135    quad[sectx][secty] = ship;
136    newqad(0);
```

`quadx`/`quady` move at 123-124; `quad[][]` is not refilled until
`newqad(0)` at 136. The `proutn`/`cramlc`/`skip(1)` between them ca

═══ #147 ═══
No static analyser runs anywhere, so verifier.md's step 2 never happens
## Problem

`.claude/agents/verifier.md` step 2 asks for static analysis:

> If `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, or `scan-build` is installed, run it over
> the changed files; if none is installed, report that as an environment
> gap rather than silently skipping.

The conditional is doing all the work. None of the three is installed on
the development machine, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` installs only
`libncurses-dev` and `tmux` — so **no static analyser runs anywhere in
this project**, on any machine, ever. The `verifier` reports the gap
honestly every time, exactly as instructed, and the gap never closes.

Across the passes on #90, #125 and #118 (PRs #142, #143, #144) that
report appeared in every single `verifier` run.

## Why it matters

The brief is written as though this leg of verification exists. It does
not, and a reader of `verifier.md` would reasonably believe otherwise —

(clean)
91fbe91 chore(gitignore): ignore the .trk files the game writes where it plays (#161)
═══ #154 full ═══
## Problem

The full-screen decision is made once, at startup, and never revisited.
`tui_init()` is called at `sst.c:462`, before the play-again loop that
begins at `sst.c:522`. So a player who starts on a terminal too small
for the panels, enlarges it, finishes the game and answers yes to "Do
you want to play again?" gets **another classic game** — on a terminal
that would now hold the panels perfectly well.

Nothing says so at that moment. The notice printed at startup has long
since scrolled away, and the second game simply begins without panels.

## Why it is worth doing now

Before #150 nobody reached this: enlarging the terminal ended the game
outright, so there was no play-again prompt to answer. Fixing that made
the sequence — enlarge, finish, play again — an ordinary thing a player
can do, and it is the sequence most likely to follow the message telling
them the terminal is too small.

`sst.doc` and `README.md` were extended in that change to say the choice
lasts for the session, and the on-screen notice now says "restart sst at
72x24 to get the panels". Those are honest descriptions of a limitation
rather than of a decision anyone made. Retrying would let all three say
something better.

## How to see it

```sh
tmux -f /dev/null -L scratch new-session -d -x 70 -y 20 -s t './build/debug/sst -t tournament 7 short novice pw'
# "Terminal too small (need 72x24) -- using classic display."
tmux -f /dev/null -L scratch send-keys -t t 'quit' Enter
tmux -f /dev/null -L scratch resize-window -t t -x 100 -y 30
# answer the score question, then "Do you want to play again?" with y
tmux -f /dev/null -L scratch capture-pane -t t -p     # classic, no panels, no notice
tmux -f /dev/null -L scratch kill-server
```

Your own socket (`-L`) as above, never the default one, and never a bare
`tmux kill-server`.

## Suggested approach

Two sizes of answer, and the smaller may be enough:

- **Reprint the notice** for a second game that is still classic, so the
  player is told rather than left to notice. Cheap, and it makes the
  current behaviour honest.
- **Retry `tui_init()`** per game. Better for the player, but it needs
  care: the panels' state, `tui_active`, and what happens if the second
  attempt fails where the first succeeded (a terminal shrunk between
  games) all have to be worked out, and `tui_shutdown()` is currently
  wired to `atexit` and to `tui_gameover()`.

Whichever, `sst.doc:1547-1550`, `README.md`'s fallback paragraph and the
second line of the startup notice all describe the present behaviour and
would need to move with it.

## Where it was found

By the `ui-review` sub-agent while reviewing the fix for #150, as the
player action that fix newly makes possible. Filed rather than folded in
per AGENTS.md step 9 — #150 is about two readers misreading an
interrupted read, and this is a different decision in a different place.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).

startdir="$srcdir"

# --- terminals the full-screen display cannot use --------------------
# Only a pty reaches these. The piped journey covers the no-terminal
# case; the terminfo probe and the size check need a real terminal that
# curses can ask about and still turn down. Each has to fall back to the
# classic display and keep playing rather than exit, hang, or draw a
# screen that never fills in.
#
# $1 description, $2 cols, $3 rows, $4 expected notice, $5 env prefix.
fallback() {
	start "$2" "$3" '' "$5"
	# Searched through the scrollback: the notice prints before the
	# banner, and on a 20-row terminal there is not much room between
	# them. A line added to the preamble later would push it off the
	# visible screen and turn this into a mystery.
	if ! wait_scrollback "$4"; then
		fail "$1: no notice that the full-screen display was refused"
		dump_scrollback
		return
	fi
	unwanted "$1: drew the panels on a terminal it had refused" " Quadrant "
	if ! wait_for 'regular, tournament, or frozen'; then
		fail "$1: the classic display did not carry on to a prompt"
		dump
		return
	fi
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'regular' Enter
	expect "$1: the classic display did not take an answer" 'Short, Medium, or Long'
}

# TERM=dumb is what Emacs' shell buffer sets: curses starts happily on
# it and then cannot address the cursor, so the game would look hung.
fallback "TERM=dumb" 80 24 "cannot do full-screen mode" 'env TERM=dumb'
# Smaller than the panels need. 72x24 is the floor; 70x20 is under it.
fallback "undersized terminal" 70 20 "Terminal too small" ''

# --- the fallback leaves no curses signal handler behind ---------------
# tui_init() calls initscr() before it can know the terminal is too
# small for the panels, and endwin() does not take back the SIGWINCH
# handler initscr() installed. So a game that fell back to the classic
# display carried a handler for the rest of the session, where a game
# started without -t has none -- which is what made every blocking read
# in the classic path interruptible there and nowhere else. That was
# #150, fixed by retrying on EINTR in both readers; this is the cause
# behind it. #152.
#
# The retries mean there is nothing left to see in what the game prints:
# both builds behave identically. So this asks the kernel instead.
# /proc/<pid>/status gives SigCgt, the mask of signals the process has
# handlers for, and SIGWINCH is 28 -- so bit 27. Linux only; skipped
# elsewhere, since the fix is worth having either way and the rest of
# this file already runs on macOS.
#
# Three arms, because two of them cannot tell each other apart. The
# fallback game and the plain game both expect "no", so a
# sigwinch_caught() that answered "no" for any reason -- an awk slip, a
# /proc format that moved -- would satisfy both and the case would pass
# having measured nothing. The full-screen game at 80x24 is the arm that
# expects "yes": it is the one that fails if the reading stops working,
# and it pins the other half of the fix besides, that the restore runs
# only on the give-up path and leaves real curses alone.
if [ ! -r /proc/self/status ]; then
	# A developer on macOS gets a note. Linux CI does not: /proc is the
	# only way to see this, so a leg where it went missing -- hidepid, an
	# unusual container, a format that moved -- would otherwise report a
	# plain pass with the three arms silently absent, which under ctest
	# shows no output at all. Same reasoning as the tmux guard at the top
	# of this file.
	if [ -n "${CI:-}" ] && [ "$(uname -s)" = Linux ]; then
		fail "sigwinch: no readable /proc on Linux CI, so the disposition went unchecked"
	else
		printf 'note: no /proc, so the SIGWINCH disposition went unchecked\n' >&2
	fi
else
	if ! command -v pgrep >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		fail "sigwinch: pgrep is missing, so the game's process could not be found"
	fi

# the message window, so waiting for it proves the command was
	# read whole. Sampling the screen after a fixed sleep instead
	# would pass on a slow machine that had not repainted yet.
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'lrscan' Enter

# --- a second game gets its own panels -------------------------------
# Carrying the same session on through quit and into a replay. The
# panels are wired to a flag that says a game is set up; getting that
# wrong showed the next player the last player's quadrant, or an empty
# frame around a game that was running (#21).
replay_case() {
	# Up before they are down: without this the blank-panel check
	# below would also pass on a run where curses had quietly fallen
	# back to the classic display.
	expect_status "replay: the panels were not up before quitting" "Stardate"
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'quit' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'score recorded'; then
		fail "replay: quit did not reach the end-of-game questions"
		dump
		return
	fi
	# The panels are blank behind these questions. Quitting is an
	# ending like any other, and the ended game has no business still
	# being framed above the score.
	wait_gone_status "replay: the quit game is still on the panels" "Stardate"
	#
	# Answered "no" deliberately: "yes" writes a save file and stops
	# to ask what to call it, stranding the test at that prompt.
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'n' Enter
	expect "replay: never asked about another game" 'play again'
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'y' Enter
	if ! wait_for 'regular, tournament, or frozen'; then
		fail "replay: the second game never started"
		dump
		return
	fi
	# And still blank through the second game's setup questions, which
	# is where the last captain's quadrant used to be framed above
	# someone else's answers (#21). setup() is what clears it.
	wait_gone "replay: the last game is still on the panels during setup" "Stardate"
	# No banner this time, so nothing has overflowed the window -- but
	# the pager stays armed from the first game, and a pause here
	# would eat this answer just the same.
	unwanted "replay: paused before the second game's first question" "CONTINUE"

	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'regular' Enter
	expect "replay: the second game lost the first answer" 'Short, Medium, or Long'
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'short' Enter
	expect "replay: setup did not reach the skill question" 'Novice, Fair, Good, Expert'
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'novice' Enter
	sleep 0.5
	tm send-keys -t "$pane" 'xyz' Enter
	if ! to_command; then
		fail "replay: the second game never reached its prompt"
		dump
		return
	fi
	# And back on for the new one.
	want_quadtitle "replay: the quadrant panel is not showing a quadrant"
	expect_status "replay: the status panel is empty" "Stardate"
}

# Only if there is a game to quit out of; otherwise 'quit' goes into
# whatever prompt is up and buries the real failure in noise.

# The mirror of wait_col_clean: wait for column $1 to carry something on
# some row from $2 to $3. Used for the precondition of a check that the
# column comes clean, where asking once races the render it is waiting
# for.
#
# No row-count guard, because this one cannot pass without a row: it
# succeeds only on having seen a character.
wait_col_dirty() {
	i=0
	while [ "$i" -lt 40 ]; do
		screen | awk -v col="$1" -v lo="$2" -v hi="$3" '
			NR >= lo && NR <= hi {
				c = substr($0, col, 1)
				if (c != "" && c != " ") seen = 1
			}
			END { exit seen ? 0 : 1 }' && return 0
		i=$((i + 1))
		sleep 0.1
	done
	return 1
}

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it
straight away — while the game is waiting for you to answer, and while
it is waiting for a keystroke at a pause — and both the question you
were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so
long as there is still room for them. Older text that no longer fits
scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.

Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for, they clip rather
than rearrange themselves. A line with more to show than there is room
for ends in `>`, so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small
one, and a heading with no room left is dropped rather than shortened.
A terminal too short for the panels is the panels' problem, not the
conversation's: they lose rows off the bottom, the grid keeping its
numbering for as long as it has rows to number, and the conversation
keeps three rows down to six — two of it and the line the prompt or the
pager sits on. Below six there is not that much left to divide and it
keeps what there is: two rows at five and one at four. So the prompt
stays on screen down to four rows, and down to six a paged command shows
a line of itself before stopping to ask — at five its one line goes to
the blank that `lrscan`, `chart` and `status` open with, though
`srscan`, which has none, still shows a line there, and at four the
pager takes the only row and a paged command shows nothing of itself at
all. Shorter than four the panels have taken the screen: the game still
reads what you type, with nothing on it to say so.

Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the
squeeze went: they redraw from the game state, so they return full of
live readings. The conversation cannot be rebuilt that way — curses
does not reflow it — so whatever scrolled away while the window was
small is gone for good, and an older line that was cut short stays cut
short. Every reading is a command away, though, and none of them costs
anything: `srscan`, `status`, `chart`, `damages`.

The line you are on usually comes back, and it is the one that matters:
a question or a pause the game was part way through writing is written
out again whole once there is room for it, so you are not left typing
into the tail of a prompt. A few prompts finish their line before they
stop to wait; those come back too, with the answer going on the row
below the question — or after it, where the window is down to its last
row.
Only their final line comes back, so a question asked over several
lines returns as the last of them. An answer you had already started
typing usually comes back with its question, on the row below it. You
may get back only one of them. Where the question ended its own line the
two sit on separate rows, so a wrapped answer needs three rows and a
window of one or two — five rows or fewer — cannot hold the pair; a
question that has itself wrapped needs a row more again. The question is
what goes, leaving your own typing with nothing above it to say what it
answers, and on a very wide terminal it is the answer that goes instead,
however tall the window is. Shorter still and only part of whichever
survived is left, and sometimes neither comes back, leaving older
conversation on screen with the game waiting behind it.

When the question and everything you typed are both on screen, carry on
and answer — that is the ordinary case now. When they are not, give the
terminal another row or two first: that usually brings it back with
your typing untouched, which beats retyping it. A very wide terminal is
the exception — more rows will not bring the answer back there, though
making it narrow enough will.

If it does not come back, or the terminal cannot grow, do not just
answer it, and do not press Enter either: whatever you typed is still
in the buffer, and a yes/no question reads the *first* letter, so an
`N` typed after a `y` you cannot see answers yes.
Press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away, and then answer. What
you type lands on whatever the window happens to be showing; the line
it fell on clears when you press Enter, though the characters you
typed stay where they landed.

If the prompt is missing or cut off and you had not started answering
it, press Enter. Nothing waiting behind one commits you to anything
then: a pause moves on, the self-destruct password reads the empty
answer as a refusal and stands the sequence down, and a yes/no
question comes back only as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, without
saying again what it asked — answer `N` there and you are back at the
prompt, free to give the command again.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead, and
stays classic for the rest of the session: the choice is made once at
startup, so enlarging the window afterwards will not bring the panels,
and neither will starting a second game from the play-again prompt.

### Building

The build is CMake, driven through presets:

```sh
cmake --preset debug           # or release
cmake --build --preset debug
./build/debug/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler, CMake 3.21 or newer, and ncurses
(`libncurses-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu; already present on macOS).
`ctest --preset debug` runs the test suite, which includes a full-screen
session driven through a real terminal and needs `tmux` — without it
that one test reports as skipped.

`cmake --list-presets` shows them all. There are four: `debug` and
`release`, and `ci-debug` and `ci-release`, which add `-Werror` and are
exactly what CI runs — so you can reproduce a CI warning locally rather
than discovering it in a pull request.

### Windows

There is no working Windows build at the moment.

The old instructions here were `cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c` from a
Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt. That has not worked for some
time: `tui.c` includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and `sst.c`,
`finish.c` and `osx.c` all call into it, so the full-screen display
cannot simply be left out of the file list either.

Making it work again means stubbing the display out under `#ifdef
WINDOWS` — `tui_init()` returning false, so the game always runs in its
classic scrolling form — and then actually building it on Windows to
find out what else has drifted. Nobody has a toolchain in play to check
that, so rather than leave instructions that fail, this says so.

input.prompt:
Review the user-facing behaviour of the change on branch `feat/tui-retry-per-game` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek. Read AGENTS.md and .claude/agents/ui-review.md.

**State:** no commits yet (HEAD `91fbe91` = `main`); unstaged changes in `sst.c`, `tui.c`, `tests/tui.sh`, `sst.doc`, `README.md`.

## What it does

Issue **#154**. The full-screen decision was made once, at startup (`tui_init()` at `sst.c:462`), and never revisited. A player who started on a terminal too small for the panels, grew it, finished the game and answered yes to "Do you want to play again?" got **another classic game** on a terminal that would now hold the panels — and nothing on screen said so, the startup notice having scrolled away a game ago.

Now `tui_init()` is retried once per game, at the foot of the play-again loop (`sst.c:542`, after `if (!ja()) break;`). Deliberately not per resize: mid-game is the one time there is a game on screen to lose.

Two things had to be fixed inside `tui_init()` to make a second call work at all, both measured against ncurses 6.6.20251231:

- A second `initscr()` reports the **stale** size — started at 70x20 and grown to 100x30, it still says 20x70, `is_term_resized()` agrees nothing changed, and `resize_term(0, 0)` leaves it there. So the retry would turn itself down. Fixed by asking the tty directly (`TIOCGWINSZ`) and `resize_term()`ing to that.
- ncurses installs its SIGWINCH handler once per process, so after #152's give-up path restored the old disposition, a second `initscr()` gets **none** — a terminal resized under `getch()` then produces no `KEY_RESIZE` and no keypress either, so the read just stays blocked. Fixed by capturing curses' own handler at the first `initscr()` and re-installing it.

## What a player sees differently

1. **The startup notice's second line changed.** Was `It stays classic: restart sst at 72x24 to get the panels.` (57 cols). Now `Grow it to 72x24 and the next game gets the panels.` (51 cols). The first line is unchanged at 57 columns: `Terminal too small (need 72x24) -- using classic display.` Both counts are measured, not asserted. Please judge the new line as a player reads it — is "the next game" unambiguous, given this game asks "Do you want to play again?" and a player might equally read it as "next time I run sst"? Both are in fact true now, which may be what makes it safe, or may be what makes it vague.
2. **Panels can appear between games.** Grow the terminal, answer yes, and the second game comes up full-screen where the first was classic.
3. **A failed retry is silent** — still too small, so it stays classic and does not repeat the notice.

## What I checked myself, and what I want you to judge

- Plain mode (no `-t`) is byte-identical: deterministic `tournament 7` journey, 81 lines, no diff against `main`.
- TUI at 80x24 and 72x24: panels draw correctly, the ioctl is a no-op on the first init.
- The failed-retry path at 70x20 stays playable — setup questions continue and take answers.  *
 * The pure formatting functions live in tuifmt.c so they can be unit
 * tested without curses; the curses backend itself lives in tui.c.
 *
 * Self-contained on purpose: including this must not oblige a file to
 * include sst.h as well. See the note on tui_active below.

#ifndef SST_TUI_H
#define SST_TUI_H

			   where tui.c starts colouring the value */

/* What a grid cell and a status line are, for colouring.
 *
 * A cell is classified from the character the panel is about to show,
 * never from the game state behind it. When the sensors are damaged
 * every hidden cell reads as '-', so they all classify alike and
 * colour cannot become a way to see what a scan is hiding. */
enum cellclass {
	CELL_PLAIN,	/* empty space, grid labels */
	CELL_HOSTILE,	/* Klingons, Commanders, Romulans, Tholians */
	CELL_SHIP,	/* ours */
	CELL_BASE,
	CELL_STAR,
	CELL_PLANET,
	CELL_WEB,
	CELL_THING,	/* the unknown object Spock tells you to look at */
	CELL_HIDDEN	/* masked by damaged sensors */
};

enum statusclass {
	STAT_PLAIN,
	STAT_GOOD,
	STAT_WARN,
	STAT_BAD,
	STAT_DOCKED
};

/* Panel formatters (tuifmt.c). Both read the global game state. */
void fmt_quad_line(int i, char *buf);	/* i=0 header, 1..10 grid rows */
void fmt_status_line(int i, char *buf);	/* i=1..10, srscan status fields */

int status_class(int i);		/* colour class of a status line */

 * EXTERN/INCLUDED trick that instantiates the game state: these two
 * describe the display, not the game, and keeping them out of it is
 * what lets this header stand on its own. osx.c needs that -- it wants

# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it
straight away — while the game is waiting for you to answer, and while
it is waiting for a keystroke at a pause — and both the question you
were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so
long as there is still room for them. Older text that no longer fits
scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.

Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for, they clip rather
than rearrange themselves. A line with more to show than there is room
for ends in `>`, so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small
one, and a heading with no room left is dropped rather than shortened.
A terminal too short for the panels is the panels' problem, not the
conversation's: they lose rows off the bottom, the grid keeping its
numbering for as long as it has rows to number, and the conversation
keeps three rows down to six — two of it and the line the prompt or the
pager sits on. Below six there is not that much left to divide and it
keeps what there is: two rows at five and one at four. So the prompt
stays on screen down to four rows, and down to six a paged command shows
a line of itself before stopping to ask — at five its one line goes to
the blank that `lrscan`, `chart` and `status` open with, though
`srscan`, which has none, still shows a line there, and at four the
pager takes the only row and a paged command shows nothing of itself at
all. Shorter than four the panels have taken the screen: the game still
reads what you type, with nothing on it to say so.

Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the
squeeze went: they redraw from the game state, so they return full of
live readings. The conversation cannot be rebuilt that way — curses
does not reflow it — so whatever scrolled away while the window was
small is gone for good, and an older line that was cut short stays cut
short. Every reading is a command away, though, and none of them costs
anything: `srscan`, `status`, `chart`, `damages`.

The line you are on usually comes back, and it is the one that matters:
a question or a pause the game was part way through writing is written
out again whole once there is room for it, so you are not left typing
into the tail of a prompt. A few prompts finish their line before they
stop to wait; those come back too, with the answer going on the row
below the question — or after it, where the window is down to its last
row.
Only their final line comes back, so a question asked over several
lines returns as the last of them. An answer you had already started
typing usually comes back with its question, on the row below it. You
may get back only one of them. Where the question ended its own line the
two sit on separate rows, so a wrapped answer needs three rows and a
window of one or two — five rows or fewer — cannot hold the pair; a
question that has itself wrapped needs a row more again. The question is
what goes, leaving your own typing with nothing above it to say what it
answers, and on a very wide terminal it is the answer that goes instead,
however tall the window is. Shorter still and only part of whichever
survived is left, and sometimes neither comes back, leaving older
conversation on screen with the game waiting behind it.

When the question and everything you typed are both on screen, carry on
and answer — that is the ordinary case now. When they are not, give the
terminal another row or two first: that usually brings it back with
your typing untouched, which beats retyping it. A very wide terminal is
the exception — more rows will not bring the answer back there, though
making it narrow enough will.

If it does not come back, or the terminal cannot grow, do not just
answer it, and do not press Enter either: whatever you typed is still
in the buffer, and a yes/no question reads the *first* letter, so an
`N` typed after a `y` you cannot see answers yes.
Press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away, and then answer. What
you type lands on whatever the window happens to be showing; the line
it fell on clears when you press Enter, though the characters you
typed stay where they landed.

If the prompt is missing or cut off and you had not started answering
it, press Enter. Nothing waiting behind one commits you to anything
then: a pause moves on, the self-destruct password reads the empty
answer as a refusal and stands the sequence down, and a yes/no
question comes back only as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, without
saying again what it asked — answer `N` there and you are back at the
prompt, free to give the command again.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead. That
game stays classic to the end — enlarging the window will not bring the
panels up part way through it.

The choice is made again for each game, though. So if the terminal was
too small and you have since made it bigger, answering yes to "Do you
want to play again?" starts the next game with the panels. A terminal
that is still too small stays classic, and does not say so a second
time.

### Building

The build is CMake, driven through presets:

```sh
cmake --preset debug           # or release
cmake --build --preset debug
./build/debug/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler, CMake 3.21 or newer, and ncurses
(`libncurses-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu; already present on macOS).
`ctest --preset debug` runs the test suite, which includes a full-screen
session driven through a real terminal and needs `tmux` — without it
that one test reports as skipped.

`cmake --list-presets` shows them all. There are four: `debug` and
`release`, and `ci-debug` and `ci-release`, which add `-Werror` and are
exactly what CI runs — so you can reproduce a CI warning locally rather
than discovering it in a pull request.

### Windows

There is no working Windows build at the moment.

The old instructions here were `cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c` from a
Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt. That has not worked for some
time: `tui.c` includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and `sst.c`,
`finish.c` and `osx.c` all call into it, so the full-screen display
cannot simply be left out of the file list either.

Making it work again means stubbing the display out under `#ifdef
WINDOWS` — `tui_init()` returning false, so the game always runs in its
classic scrolling form — and then actually building it on Windows to
find out what else has drifted. Nobody has a toolchain in play to check
that, so rather than leave instructions that fail, this says so.

content.text:
## Verdict

Acceptable as-is, with one message-content improvement I'd like you to weigh. Everything from round one landed: the diagnostic fires exactly when the player moved the terminal and stays silent when they didn't, across a three-game sequence; the retry line lands on its own line, cleanly separated from the `y` echo above it and the `Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?` below it, so it does *not* get swallowed the way the end-of-game questions run together; "staying classic" reads fine given that the startup notice has already introduced both "classic display" and "panels"; and the ioctl change is a visible improvement on the first game (I reproduced the corrupted grid on the pre-change binary under `LINES=50 COLUMNS=200` and a clean one after) with byte-identical panes at 80x24, 72x24 and 100x30 otherwise, and byte-identical plain-mode and piped `-t` transcripts. Your resolution of round-one finding 4 is sound and I am not pressing it — see below for why I could not find an honest cushion either. The one thing I'd still change is that the new line reports the requirement a third time but never the observation, which is the half of the tmux-status-bar confusion it was written to end.

## Findings

**1. should-fix — the retry line repeats the requirement but never says what the game measured.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c:555`

A player who grew a tmux pane to what they believe is 80x24 and lost a row to the status bar now sees, for the third time in the session, the number `72x24`. What they have never been shown is the number the game is comparing it against. Your own comment states the goal — they "ha[ve] no way to tell a mis-sized window from a broken promise" — and the line as written closes only half of that: it proves the game noticed the resize, but leaves the player re-measuring a window they already believe is right. `README.md` and `sst.doc` explain the status-bar row, but a player mid-session is not reading either.

The size is already in hand: `refusedlines`/`refusedcols` are set on the failed retry to the size just refused, `proutf` takes a format, and the game already prints formatted numbers everywhere else. Suggestion, with an accessor such as `tui_refused_size(&cols, &rows)`:

```
Terminal is 80x23 -- need 72x24, staying classic.
```

That is 48 columns at two-digit sizes and 49 at `100x23`, so it stays inside the 57-column budget the other two lines hold. Avoid phrasing it as "still under 72x24": at `100x23` the terminal is not under 72 columns, and a player reading that would go widen the wrong axis.

If you'd rather keep the line short and symmetrical with the startup pair, resolving this explicitly is defensible — the current line is correct and understandable. I'm grading it should-fix because it is the one piece of information the player cannot get any other way without leaving the game.

**2. nit — README states the per-game re-choice unconditionally, and the reverse direction does not happen.** `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/README.md:101`

"The choice is made again for each game, though." is true only while the current game is classic; the retry is gated on `!tui_active`. I verified the other direction: started at 100x30 with panels, quit, answered no to the score question, shrank the pane to 60x16, answered yes — the second game came up in clipped panels, not classic. That is the right behavior and matches `sst.doc`'s "never drops it back to the classic display, at any point", but the README has no counterbalancing sentence anywhere near line 101, so a reader who shrinks between games is set up to expect classic. `sst.doc:1553` carries the same sentence but is rescued by the paragraph immediately after it, so this is mostly a README problem.

Suggestion: scope the sentence, e.g. "If a game went classic, the choice is made again for the next one" — or add the half-sentence the README is missing: panels, once up, stay up for the rest of the session however you resize.

**3. nit (optional) — the ioctl now overrides exported `LINES`/`COLUMNS`, and nothing player-facing says so.**

Confirmed both halves of your measurement. The corrupted-grid case is a clear win. The flip side is that a player who deliberately exported a smaller `LINES`/`COLUMNS` to keep the display compact now silently gets the full terminal. Neither `README.md` nor `sst.doc` has ever mentioned those variables, so nothing documented is broken and I would not spend `sst.doc` space on it — but if you want it on the record for players rather than only in the commit, one clause in the `-t` section ("`-t` asks the terminal its size, so exported `LINES`/`COLUMNS` do not change the display") would do it.

## Answers to your four questions

- **Where the line lands.** It reads well. The stream is `Do you want to play again?y` / `Terminal still too small (need 72x24) -- staying classic.` / `Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?` — the new line is the only thing between the commitment and the first setup question, on its own line, with nothing else competing. It does not get lost the way `Do you want your score recorded?Do you want to play again?` runs together, because both of its neighbours are line-terminated on that side. At 50 columns it wraps mid-word (`staying c` / `lassic.`), which is exactly the same shape the startup line already has there, so nothing new.
- **"staying classic".** Understandable. By the time it prints, the player has seen "using classic display" and "the next game gets panels" in the same session, so both nouns are established and "staying classic" reads as the natural echo of the first. Keeping "panels" over "full-screen" is right — it matches both docs, and the pairing of "using classic display" / "staying classic" is the strongest argument for it.

/* What a grid cell and a status line are, for colouring.
 *
 * A cell is classified from the character the panel is about to show,
 * never from the game state behind it. When the sensors are damaged
 * every hidden cell reads as '-', so they all classify alike and
 * colour cannot become a way to see what a scan is hiding. */
enum cellclass {
	CELL_PLAIN,	/* empty space, grid labels */
	CELL_HOSTILE,	/* Klingons, Commanders, Romulans, Tholians */
	CELL_SHIP,	/* ours */
	CELL_BASE,
	CELL_STAR,
	CELL_PLANET,
	CELL_WEB,

	CELL_HIDDEN	/* masked by damaged sensors */
};

	STAT_GOOD,

	STAT_BAD,

# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it
straight away — while the game is waiting for you to answer, and while
it is waiting for a keystroke at a pause — and both the question you
were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so
long as there is still room for them. Older text that no longer fits
scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.

Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for, they clip rather
than rearrange themselves. A line with more to show than there is room
for ends in `>`, so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small
one, and a heading with no room left is dropped rather than shortened.
A terminal too short for the panels is the panels' problem, not the
conversation's: they lose rows off the bottom, the grid keeping its
numbering for as long as it has rows to number, and the conversation
keeps three rows down to six — two of it and the line the prompt or the
pager sits on. Below six there is not that much left to divide and it
keeps what there is: two rows at five and one at four. So the prompt
stays on screen down to four rows, and down to six a paged command shows
a line of itself before stopping to ask — at five its one line goes to
the blank that `lrscan`, `chart` and `status` open with, though
`srscan`, which has none, still shows a line there, and at four the
pager takes the only row and a paged command shows nothing of itself at
all. Shorter than four the panels have taken the screen: the game still
reads what you type, with nothing on it to say so.

Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the
squeeze went: they redraw from the game state, so they return full of
live readings. The conversation cannot be rebuilt that way — curses
does not reflow it — so whatever scrolled away while the window was
small is gone for good, and an older line that was cut short stays cut
short. Every reading is a command away, though, and none of them costs
anything: `srscan`, `status`, `chart`, `damages`.

The line you are on usually comes back, and it is the one that matters:
a question or a pause the game was part way through writing is written
out again whole once there is room for it, so you are not left typing
into the tail of a prompt. A few prompts finish their line before they
stop to wait; those come back too, with the answer going on the row
below the question — or after it, where the window is down to its last
row.
Only their final line comes back, so a question asked over several
lines returns as the last of them. An answer you had already started
typing usually comes back with its question, on the row below it. You
may get back only one of them. Where the question ended its own line the
two sit on separate rows, so a wrapped answer needs three rows and a
window of one or two — five rows or fewer — cannot hold the pair; a
question that has itself wrapped needs a row more again. The question is
what goes, leaving your own typing with nothing above it to say what it
answers, and on a very wide terminal it is the answer that goes instead,
however tall the window is. Shorter still and only part of whichever
survived is left, and sometimes neither comes back, leaving older
conversation on screen with the game waiting behind it.

When the question and everything you typed are both on screen, carry on
and answer — that is the ordinary case now. When they are not, give the
terminal another row or two first: that usually brings it back with
your typing untouched, which beats retyping it. A very wide terminal is
the exception — more rows will not bring the answer back there, though
making it narrow enough will.

If it does not come back, or the terminal cannot grow, do not just
answer it, and do not press Enter either: whatever you typed is still
in the buffer, and a yes/no question reads the *first* letter, so an
`N` typed after a `y` you cannot see answers yes.
Press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away, and then answer. What
you type lands on whatever the window happens to be showing; the line
it fell on clears when you press Enter, though the characters you
typed stay where they landed.

If the prompt is missing or cut off and you had not started answering
it, press Enter. Nothing waiting behind one commits you to anything
then: a pause moves on, the self-destruct password reads the empty
answer as a refusal and stands the sequence down, and a yes/no
question comes back only as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, without
saying again what it asked — answer `N` there and you are back at the
prompt, free to give the command again.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead. That
game stays classic to the end — enlarging the window will not bring the
panels up part way through it.

The choice is made again for each game, though. So if the terminal was
too small and you have since made it bigger, answering yes to "Do you
want to play again?" starts the next game with the panels. If you
resized it and it is still too small, the game says so rather than
leaving you to wonder — 72x24 is the whole of what it takes, and a tmux
status bar can cost you the row that decides it. Leave the terminal
alone and it stays quiet: you were told at startup and nothing has
changed since.

### Building

The build is CMake, driven through presets:

```sh
cmake --preset debug           # or release
cmake --build --preset debug
./build/debug/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler, CMake 3.21 or newer, and ncurses
(`libncurses-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu; already present on macOS).
`ctest --preset debug` runs the test suite, which includes a full-screen
session driven through a real terminal and needs `tmux` — without it
that one test reports as skipped.

`cmake --list-presets` shows them all. There are four: `debug` and
`release`, and `ci-debug` and `ci-release`, which add `-Werror` and are
exactly what CI runs — so you can reproduce a CI warning locally rather
than discovering it in a pull request.

### Windows

There is no working Windows build at the moment.

The old instructions here were `cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c` from a
Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt. That has not worked for some
time: `tui.c` includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and `sst.c`,
`finish.c` and `osx.c` all call into it, so the full-screen display
cannot simply be left out of the file list either.

Making it work again means stubbing the display out under `#ifdef
WINDOWS` — `tui_init()` returning false, so the game always runs in its
classic scrolling form — and then actually building it on Windows to
find out what else has drifted. Nobody has a toolchain in play to check
that, so rather than leave instructions that fail, this says so.

## Verdict
