# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option (`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it
straight away — while the game is waiting for you to answer, and while
it is waiting for a keystroke at a pause — and both the question you
were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so
long as there is still room for them. Older text that no longer fits
scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.

Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for, they clip rather
than rearrange themselves. A line with more to show than there is room
for ends in `>`, so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small
one, and a heading with no room left is dropped rather than shortened.
A terminal too short for the panels is the panels' problem, not the
conversation's: they lose rows off the bottom, the grid keeping its
numbering for as long as it has rows to number, and the conversation
keeps three rows down to six — two of it and the line the prompt or the
pager sits on. Below six there is not that much left to divide and it
keeps what there is: two rows at five and one at four. So the prompt
stays on screen down to four rows, and down to six a paged command shows
a line of itself before stopping to ask — at five its one line goes to
the blank that `lrscan`, `chart` and `status` open with, though
`srscan`, which has none, still shows a line there, and at four the
pager takes the only row and a paged command shows nothing of itself at
all. Shorter than four the panels have taken the screen: the game still
reads what you type, with nothing on it to say so.

Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the
squeeze went: they redraw from the game state, so they return full of
live readings. The conversation cannot be rebuilt that way — curses
does not reflow it — so whatever scrolled away while the window was
small is gone for good, and an older line that was cut short stays cut
short. Every reading is a command away, though, and none of them costs
anything: `srscan`, `status`, `chart`, `damages`.

The line you are on usually comes back, and it is the one that matters:
a question or a pause the game was part way through writing is written
out again whole once there is room for it, so you are not left typing
into the tail of a prompt. A few prompts finish their line before they
stop to wait; those come back too, with the answer going on the row
below the question — or after it, where the window is down to its last
row.
Only their final line comes back, so a question asked over several
lines returns as the last of them. An answer you had already started
typing usually comes back with its question, on the row below it. You
may get back only one of them. Where the question ended its own line the
two sit on separate rows, so a wrapped answer needs three rows and a
window of one or two — five rows or fewer — cannot hold the pair; a
question that has itself wrapped needs a row more again. The question is
what goes, leaving your own typing with nothing above it to say what it
answers, and on a very wide terminal it is the answer that goes instead,
however tall the window is. Shorter still and only part of whichever
survived is left, and sometimes neither comes back, leaving older
conversation on screen with the game waiting behind it.

When the question and everything you typed are both on screen, carry on
and answer — that is the ordinary case now. When they are not, give the
terminal another row or two first: that usually brings it back with
your typing untouched, which beats retyping it. A very wide terminal is
the exception — more rows will not bring the answer back there, though
making it narrow enough will.

If it does not come back, or the terminal cannot grow, do not just
answer it, and do not press Enter either: whatever you typed is still
in the buffer, and a yes/no question reads the *first* letter, so an
`N` typed after a `y` you cannot see answers yes.
Press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away, and then answer. What
you type lands on whatever the window happens to be showing; the line
it fell on clears when you press Enter, though the characters you
typed stay where they landed.

If the prompt is missing or cut off and you had not started answering
it, press Enter. Nothing waiting behind one commits you to anything
then: a pause moves on, the self-destruct password reads the empty
answer as a refusal and stands the sequence down, and a yes/no
question comes back only as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, without
saying again what it asked — answer `N` there and you are back at the
prompt, free to give the command again.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead. That
game stays classic to the end — enlarging the window will not bring the
panels up part way through it.

A game that went classic gets the choice made again for the next one,
though. So if the terminal was too small and you have since made it
bigger, answering yes to "Do you want to play again?" starts the next
game with the panels. If you resized it and it is still too small, the
game says what size it read back rather than leaving you to wonder —
72x24 is the whole of what it takes, and a tmux status bar can cost you
the row that decides it. Leave the terminal alone and it stays quiet:
you were told at startup and nothing has changed since.

It only goes that way. Panels that are up stay up for the rest of the
session however you resize, as above: they clip rather than give way to
the classic display.

The size comes from the terminal itself rather than from `LINES` and
`COLUMNS`, so exporting those does not make the display smaller.

### Building

The build is CMake, driven through presets:

```sh
cmake --preset debug           # or release
cmake --build --preset debug
./build/debug/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler, CMake 3.21 or newer, and ncurses
(`libncurses-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu; already present on macOS).
`ctest --preset debug` runs the test suite, which includes a full-screen
session driven through a real terminal and needs `tmux` — without it
that one test reports as skipped.

`cmake --list-presets` shows them all. There are four: `debug` and
`release`, and `ci-debug` and `ci-release`, which add `-Werror` and are
exactly what CI runs — so you can reproduce a CI warning locally rather
than discovering it in a pull request.

### Windows

There is no working Windows build at the moment.

The old instructions here were `cl /DWINDOWS /Fesst.exe *.c` from a
Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt. That has not worked for some
time: `tui.c` includes `<curses.h>` unconditionally, and `sst.c`,
`finish.c` and `osx.c` all call into it, so the full-screen display
cannot simply be left out of the file list either.

Making it work again means stubbing the display out under `#ifdef
WINDOWS` — `tui_init()` returning false, so the game always runs in its
classic scrolling form — and then actually building it on Windows to
find out what else has drifted. Nobody has a toolchain in play to check
that, so rather than leave instructions that fail, this says so.

The three output helpers in `sst.c` pair up by name, but not by

| function | ends the line? |
| --- | --- |
| `proutn(s)` | no |
| `prout(s)` | **yes** -- it is literally `proutn(s); skip(1);` |
| `proutf(fmt, ...)` | **no** |

is "`prout` with a format". It is not: it ends with

```c

```

so a format string with no trailing `\n` leaves the line open. The
formatted counterpart of `prout` does not exist, and the one that does
is named as though it were.

It misleads, and it has. While implementing #154 I replaced a `prout`
with a `proutf` to interpolate two numbers into a notice, and the notice
ran into the question after it:

```
Terminal is 80x22 -- need 72x24, staying classic.Would you like a regular, tourn
ament, or frozen game?
```

That reached a review round before a test caught it -- and caught it
sideways, by failing on the *wrapped question* rather than on the
notice.

It is visible in shipped output too. The end-of-game questions share a
line for the same reason (`sst.c:528` and `sst.c:534` are both `proutf`
with no `\n`):

```
Do you want your score recorded?Do you want to play again?
```

`tests/golden/ending.txt` and `tests/golden/combat.txt` both record that
shape, so it is long-established rather than new. On a real terminal the
echoed answer partly hides it; under piped input it does not.

## Where it was found

By `ui-review` on the #154 branch, as the pre-existing run-on sitting
two lines above the notice that change adds. Filed rather than fixed
there, per AGENTS.md step 9 -- #154 is about revisiting the full-screen
choice between games.

## Fixing it

The naming is the defect; what to do about the existing output is a
separate judgment.

- **Least disruptive:** leave every call site alone and document the
  asymmetry in a comment beside `proutf`, so the next person to reach
  for it is not misled. Changes no output and no fixture.
- **Consistent:** add a `proutfn` for the open-line form, make `proutf`
  end its line like `prout`, and audit the call sites. That changes the
  end-of-game questions to sit on separate lines, which means
  re-recording the golden fixtures -- with the reason in the commit, per
  the rules about the recordings, since the arithmetic is untouched and
  only the line breaks move.

Whether the run-on questions are worth changing is a display judgment
and could be split off; the misleading name can be fixed either way.

content.text:
## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed state: worktree of `feat/tui-retry-per-game` at HEAD `91fbe91` (= `main`, no commits on the branch); nothing staged, nothing untracked. Pending changes are the six modified files: `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c`, `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `tests/tui.sh`, `sst.doc`, `README.md`.

The core of #154 — the per-game retry, the SIGWINCH re-install, the refusal-size diagnostic, the three new `tui.sh` cases — is sound, and I could not break it. The problem is the out-of-scope half you disclosed: the ioctl override on the **first** call.

---

## Findings

### Blocker — the `LINES`/`COLUMNS` override gets the panels up and then leaves them deaf to every resize

`tui.c:1108-1110` (the ioctl/`resize_term` on the first call), documented at `README.md:115-116`.

Measured on a clean build of this worktree (copy outside the repo, own tmux socket, ncurses 6.6.20251231):

- `env LINES=20 COLUMNS=70`, pane 100x30: panels come up at 100x30 (the improvement you claim — confirmed, and confirmed absent on a true `HEAD` build, which falls back to classic).
- Grow the pane to 110x34: the panels **stay at 100 columns**. Instrumenting `sync_size()` shows why: `LINES=30 COLS=100 built=30x100 ioctl=34x110 resized=0` — ncurses never updates `LINES`/`COLS` when the environment pins the size, `is_term_resized()` compares against that cached size, so `sync_size()` returns early forever.
- Shrink the pane to 72x24 instead, and the 100-column panels do not clip: the top of the frame scrolls off, the status panel's right border is cut mid-row, the layout is wrecked. The identical journey **without** the env vars clips perfectly on the same build, so this is specific to the configuration the change newly admits.

So for a player with those variables exported, this diff turns "classic display, resizes fine" (what `main` gives) into "panels frozen at startup size, frame breaks on the first resize" — while `README.md:18` promises "Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it straight away", `README.md:112-113` promises panels "clip rather than give way", and `sst.doc:1556+` says the same. The sentence this diff adds at `README.md:115` invites exactly the configuration that falsifies the three sentences above it.

Suggested fix, and your own mutation proof says it is available: **apply the ioctl only on a retry**. You already measured that "making the ioctl skip its first call failed only the new `env size:` check" — i.e. everything #154 asks for still works. Gate it on `havecursewinch` (TRUE only once a first `initscr()` has happened), drop the `README.md:115-116` sentence and the "Not a no-op on the first call" paragraph at `tui.c:1088-1096`, drop the `env size:` case at `tests/tui.sh:2785`, and file the environment-versus-ioctl handling as its own issue — where the resize half can be fixed properly (`resized()`/`sync_size()` would have to take the size from the ioctl too, since `resize_term(0, 0)` cannot).

If you would rather keep it, then the first-call override needs the resize path to match, and that is a second slice, not a comment.

### Should-fix — `ui-review` never saw the one player-visible state this change creates outside #154

Three rounds are reported and their coverage is named: the diagnostic's wording, the missing measurement, the README's over-broad claim, the lost newline, and widths at 80x22 / 100x22 / 71x24 / 72x23 / 44 columns. Not one of them names the exported-`LINES`/`COLUMNS` display — which is the only *new* screen this change produces beyond the retry, and which (per the blocker) is broken. The `verifier` confirmed the direction of the behavior change but reads exit codes and text, not screens.

If the blocker is resolved by dropping the first-call override, nothing new reaches the player and no further round is owed. If you keep it, that configuration needs a `ui-review` round on it. For everything else, I accept the claim that round 3 saw the committed state: the only edit after it was the `env size:` test, which is test-only.

### Should-fix — the file now carries two opposite claims about `resize_term(0, 0)`, and the older one is false

`tui.c:918` says `resize_term(0, 0); /* adopt whatever the terminal is now */`; the new comment at `tui.c:1087` says "`resize_term(0, 0)` leaves it there". Probe against ncurses 6.6.20251231 (`initscr()` in an 80x24 pane, `resize_term(30,100)`, then `resize_term(0,0)`):

```
resize_term(30,100)=OK  LINES=30 COLS=100
resize_term(0,0)=ERR    LINES=30 COLS=100
is_term_resized(30,100)=0   is_term_resized(24,80)=1
```

`resize_term(0, 0)` is an unconditional `ERR` no-op — it adopts nothing, ever, so `tui.c:918`'s comment is wrong and `sync_size()`'s adoption is entirely ncurses' own `KEY_RESIZE` processing. The same probe shows `is_term_resized()` compares against the *cached screen size*, not the terminal, so `tui.c:308-310` ("Asked of the terminal rather than of LINES and COLS") is wrong too — and that is the mechanism behind the blocker.

Both comments are pre-existing, so under step 9 they get filed rather than fixed here (one issue covers both; `#162` is not it). What *is* in-slice: `tui.c:1086-1087` offers "resize_term(0, 0) leaves it there" as evidence that the size was cached, when it would leave anything anywhere. Reword so a later reader does not take it as a fact about the retry.

### Nit — the new test asserts the env case comes up and nothing about what happens next

`tests/tui.sh:2785-2793` checks `want_quadtitle` and stops. Had it resized afterwards — the shape every other panel case in the file uses — it would have caught the blocker. If the first-call override survives in any form, this case needs a resize arm.

---

## Checked and clean (so you do not re-derive it)

- **A second *successful* `tui_init()` is unreachable**, so `atexit(tui_shutdown)` and `make_windows()` keep their one-call assumption. `tui_active` is cleared only in `tui_shutdown()`, whose three callers are `sst.c:571` (after the loop), `sst.c:769` (followed immediately by `exit(0)`), and `atexit`. Your reasoning holds as a fact about the call graph, not just an intention.
- **Repeated failing `initscr()`/`endwin()` leaks ~0.6 KB a time** (measured: 64 KB RSS over 100 pairs at 80x24). Not worth acting on.
- **The statics are ordered correctly.** `refusedlines`/`refusedcols`/`cursewinch`/`havecursewinch` are zero-initialised by static storage; the only call order is `tui_size_changed_since_refusal()` before the retry and `tui_refused_size()` after it, and the retry always reaches the size gate that refreshes them — `stdio_is_terminal()` cannot newly fail once it has passed, and `tui_terminal_capable()` caches. The size printed is the size measured.
- **`tui.h` is the right home** for both declarations: they sit with `tui_init`/`tui_terminal_capable`, need no `sst.h` type, and keep `tui.h` self-contained for `osx.c`.
- **Comment claims that I could measure hold.** On a genuine `HEAD` build (fresh configure — a copied `build/` compiles the *original's* sources and silently produces identical binaries; I hit that trap once here): `LINES=50 COLUMNS=200` in an 80x24 pane does draw box characters smeared through the quadrant rows, and `LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` in a 100x30 pane does refuse the panels. The 57/57/49-column widths are exact, and the "at two-digit sizes" qualifier is doing real work (three digits gives 50).
- **The `unchanged:` case is not blind.** I rebuilt with the `resized` gate dropped and drove the journey at 70x20: `Terminal is 70x20 -- need 72x24, staying classic.` is on the *visible* screen when `Would you like a regular...` appears, so `unwanted`'s screen-only match discriminates. Your mutation proof stands.
- Plain mode and piped `-t` are untouched (`usetui && !tui_active`, and `tui_init()` returns at `stdio_is_terminal()` before `initscr()`); `sst.doc` is CRLF throughout with new lines ≤68 columns.

## Not reviewed

- The full `ctest`/golden/journey battery — the concurrent `verifier` owns it; I ran only targeted tmux journeys on copies outside the repository.
- The mechanism behind "the first read after a retry comes back `KEY_RESIZE`" (`tui.c:1097-1103`). The observable is harmless either way and both readers loop on it, but I did not reproduce the 410 or verify the causal attribution to the retry.

`tui.c:1108-1110` (the ioctl/`resize_term` on the first call), documented at `README.md:115-116`.

Instrumenting `sync_size()` shows why: `LINES=30 COLS=100 built=30x100 ioctl=34x110 resized=0` — ncurses never updates `LINES`/`COLS` when the environment pins the size, `is_term_resized()` compares against that cached size, so `sync_size()` returns early forever.

The identical journey **without** the env vars clips perfectly on the same build, so this is specific to the configuration the change newly admits.

You already measured that "making the ioctl skip its first call failed only the new `env size:` check" — i.e. everything #154 asks for still works. resize_term(0,0)=ERR    LINES=30 COLS=100

# tracking the terminal at all -- is_term_resized() compares against the
# pinned size, so sync_size() returns early for the rest of the session.
# Overriding them would buy panels frozen at their startup size, whose
# frame breaks rather than clips on the first resize, in place of a

# difference between the panels and the fallback.

	fail "env size: an exported 20x70 did not refuse the panels in a 100x30 terminal"
	dump_scrollback
elif ! wait_for 'COMMAND'; then
	fail "env size: the game never reached a command prompt"
	dump
fi

1	# Super Star Trek
2	
3	Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.
4	
5	Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.
6	
7	[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)
8	
9	### Full-screen mode
10	
11	Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
12	ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
13	conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
14	(columns by rows) and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option
15	(`sst -f -t`).
16	Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.
17	
18	Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it
19	straight away — while the game is waiting for you to answer, and while
20	it is waiting for a keystroke at a pause — and both the question you
21	were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so
22	long as there is still room for them. Older text that no longer fits
23	scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.
24	
25	Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for, they clip rather
26	than rearrange themselves. A line with more to show than there is room
27	for ends in `>`, so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small
28	one, and a heading with no room left is dropped rather than shortened.
29	A terminal too short for the panels is the panels' problem, not the
30	conversation's: they lose rows off the bottom, the grid keeping its
31	numbering for as long as it has rows to number, and the conversation
32	keeps three rows down to six — two of it and the line the prompt or the
33	pager sits on. Below six there is not that much left to divide and it
34	keeps what there is: two rows at five and one at four. So the prompt
35	stays on screen down to four rows, and down to six a paged command shows
36	a line of itself before stopping to ask — at five its one line goes to
37	the blank that `lrscan`, `chart` and `status` open with, though
38	`srscan`, which has none, still shows a line there, and at four the
39	pager takes the only row and a paged command shows nothing of itself at
40	all. Shorter than four the panels have taken the screen: the game still
41	reads what you type, with nothing on it to say so.
42	
43	Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the
44	squeeze went: they redraw from the game state, so they return full of
45	live readings. The conversation cannot be rebuilt that way — curses
46	does not reflow it — so whatever scrolled away while the window was
47	small is gone for good, and an older line that was cut short stays cut
48	short. Every reading is a command away, though, and none of them costs
49	anything: `srscan`, `status`, `chart`, `damages`.
50	
51	The line you are on usually comes back, and it is the one that matters:
52	a question or a pause the game was part way through writing is written
53	out again whole once there is room for it, so you are not left typing
54	into the tail of a prompt. A few prompts finish their line before they
55	stop to wait; those come back too, with the answer going on the row
56	below the question — or after it, where the window is down to its last
57	row.
58	Only their final line comes back, so a question asked over several
59	lines returns as the last of them. An answer you had already started
60	typing usually comes back with its question, on the row below it. You
61	may get back only one of them. Where the question ended its own line the
62	two sit on separate rows, so a wrapped answer needs three rows and a
63	window of one or two — five rows or fewer — cannot hold the pair; a
64	question that has itself wrapped needs a row more again. The question is
65	what goes, leaving your own typing with nothing above it to say what it
66	answers, and on a very wide terminal it is the answer that goes instead,
67	however tall the window is. Shorter still and only part of whichever
68	survived is left, and sometimes neither comes back, leaving older
69	conversation on screen with the game waiting behind it.
70	
71	When the question and everything you typed are both on screen, carry on
72	and answer — that is the ordinary case now. When they are not, give the
73	terminal another row or two first: that usually brings it back with
74	your typing untouched, which beats retyping it. A very wide terminal is
75	the exception — more rows will not bring the answer back there, though
76	making it narrow enough will.
77	
78	If it does not come back, or the terminal cannot grow, do not just
79	answer it, and do not press Enter either: whatever you typed is still
80	in the buffer, and a yes/no question reads the *first* letter, so an
81	`N` typed after a `y` you cannot see answers yes.
82	Press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away, and then answer. What
83	you type lands on whatever the window happens to be showing; the line
84	it fell on clears when you press Enter, though the characters you
85	typed stay where they landed.
86	
87	If the prompt is missing or cut off and you had not started answering
88	it, press Enter. Nothing waiting behind one commits you to anything
89	then: a pause moves on, the self-destruct password reads the empty
90	answer as a refusal and stands the sequence down, and a yes/no
91	question comes back only as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, without
92	saying again what it asked — answer `N` there and you are back at the
93	prompt, free to give the command again.
94	
95	If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
96	game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
97	no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —

101	
102	A game that went classic gets the choice made again for the next one,
103	though. So if the terminal was too small and you have since made it
104	bigger, answering yes to "Do you want to play again?" starts the next
105	game with the panels. If you resized it and it is still too small, the
106	game says what size it read back rather than leaving you to wonder —
107	72x24 is the whole of what it takes, and a tmux status bar can cost you

cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek
gh issue create --title "Two comments in tui.c describe resize_term(0,0) and is_term_resized() as doing things they do not" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

Two long-standing comments in `tui.c` state mechanisms that measurement
does not support. Both sit on the resize path, which is the most
delicate code in the file.

### 1. `tui.c:917` — `resize_term(0, 0)` adopts nothing

```c
	resize_term(0, 0);	/* adopt whatever the terminal is now */
```

`resize_term(0, 0)` is an unconditional `ERR` no-op. Measured against
ncurses 6.6.20251231 — `initscr()` in an 80x24 pane, then:

```
resize_term(30,100)=OK   LINES=30 COLS=100
resize_term(0,0)=ERR     LINES=30 COLS=100
```

It adopts nothing, ever. Whatever adoption `sync_size()` gets comes from
ncurses' own `KEY_RESIZE` processing before the call, not from the call.
So the line either wants deleting or wants a comment saying what it is
actually for.

### 2. `tui.c:307-309` — `is_term_resized()` does not ask the terminal

```c
/* Whether the terminal changed shape since the windows were built.
 * Asked of the terminal rather than of LINES and COLS: those are only
 * brought up to date when curses processes the resize, and a read that
 * came back empty needs the answer before that has happened. */
```

`is_term_resized()` compares its arguments against ncurses' **cached**
screen size, not against the terminal. From the same probe:

```
is_term_resized(30,100)=0    is_term_resized(24,80)=1
```

after `resize_term(30,100)` in an 80x24 pane — it agrees with the cache
and disagrees with the tty. The distinction the comment draws is
therefore the opposite of what happens: `LINES`/`COLS` and
`is_term_resized()` are both downstream of the same cache.

## Why it matters

The second one is not merely wrong on paper; it is the mechanism behind
a real fault. Where `LINES`/`COLUMNS` are exported, ncurses honours them
and then stops tracking the terminal, so `is_term_resized()` never
reports a change and `sync_size()` returns early for the rest of the
session. Measured: with `LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` in a pane grown from
100x30 to 110x34, the ioctl reports 110x34 and `is_term_resized()` still
says nothing changed.

That is the trap #154 walked into. Its first attempt overrode the
environment with an ioctl so a retried `tui_init()` could see the real
size, which brought the panels up in a configuration where they can
never follow a resize again — panels frozen at their startup size, the
frame breaking rather than clipping. It reads as safe if you believe
this comment. #154 now leaves the environment alone for exactly this
reason, and `tests/tui.sh` has an `env size:` case holding that line,
but the comment that made it look safe is still there for the next
person.

## Where it was found

By `code-review` on the #154 branch, which measured both claims with a
standalone ncurses probe. Filed rather than fixed there, per AGENTS.md
step 9 — both comments predate that change and neither is on its path.

## Fixing it

Correct both comments to what the probe shows, and decide what to do
with the `resize_term(0, 0)` call now that it is known to do nothing:
delete it, or replace it with a form that works if adoption was ever
wanted there. Worth checking at the same time whether anything else in
the file rests on `is_term_resized()` being a question about the
terminal — `resized()` has one caller, `sync_size()`, and its behaviour
under exported `LINES`/`COLUMNS` is the fault described above.
EOF
)"

`code-review` found a blocker that both previous `verifier` passes and three `ui-review` rounds missed, and it was mine.

The ioctl I added to defeat curses' cached size also overrode an exported `LINES`/`COLUMNS`, which ncurses honours. That looked like an improvement — it turned a corrupted grid into a correct one — but it brought the panels up in a configuration where **they can never follow a resize again**. ncurses, having honoured the environment, stops tracking the terminal: `is_term_resized()` compares against the pinned size, so `sync_size()` returns early forever. I reproduced it: with `LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` in a pane grown from 100x30 to 110x34, the ioctl reports 110x34 and `is_term_resized()` still says 0. So the panels freeze at their startup size and the frame breaks rather than clips on the first resize — worse than the classic display it replaced, and in flat contradiction of what `README.md` and `sst.doc` promise about resizing.

**The fix:** the ioctl no longer runs when either variable is set —

```c
	if (getenv("LINES") == NULL && getenv("COLUMNS") == NULL &&
	    ioctl(fileno(stdout), TIOCGWINSZ, &winsz) == 0 &&

The `env size:` case in `tests/tui.sh` now asserts the opposite of what it did — that an exported 20x70 still refuses the panels in a 100x30 terminal — and is mutation-proved by deleting the `getenv` pair, which failed that check alone. The `README.md` sentence claiming the terminal is asked rather than the environment is gone, since it is no longer true.

**Note the direction reversal:** your previous pass confirmed and bounded the `LINES`/`COLUMNS` override as an intended, disclosed improvement. It is now reverted. `main` and this branch should behave identically whenever either variable is exported, including `main`'s pre-existing corrupted grid at `LINES=50 COLUMNS=200` — that is now a documented pre-existing fault rather than something this change fixes. **Please confirm that equivalence directly**, branch against a `main` build, in both directions: `LINES=50 COLUMNS=200` in an 80x24 pane, and `LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` in a 100x30 pane.

I reviewed the worktree, read the surrounding code, and reproduced the behaviour under tmux on my own socket (`-L crv`, `-f /dev/null`, killed only that server).

## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed state: branch `feat/tui-retry-per-game`, HEAD `91fbe91` (identical to `main`, no commits), with unstaged edits to `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c`, `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `tests/tui.sh`, `sst.doc`, `README.md`. Nothing staged, nothing untracked.

The reversal you made is right for the case it was aimed at, and I confirmed the first-call behaviour with either variable set now matches `main`. But the guard was added in one of the two places that reason about size, and the other one still measures the terminal directly — which makes the new per-game notice fire forever in exactly the configuration the guard exists to protect.

## Findings

### Should-fix 1 — with `LINES`/`COLUMNS` exported, the "did the player resize?" test can never say no, so the new notice prints every game with a size that contradicts the player's window

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c:1010-1015` (`tui_size_changed_since_refusal()`) reads the terminal with `TIOCGWINSZ` and compares against `refusedlines`/`refusedcols`, which `tui.c:1119-1120` fills from curses' `LINES`/`COLS`. With either variable exported those two sources are pinned apart permanently: the ioctl reports the real pane, `LINES`/`COLS` report the environment, they never agree, so `resized` at `sst.c:553` is `TRUE` on every play-again and `sst.c:564` prints on every play-again.

Reproduced, no resize at any point, pane 100x30 throughout:

```
$ tmux ... -x 100 -y 30 "env LINES=20 COLUMNS=70 ./build/debug/sst -t tournament 7 short novice pw"

### 1. `LINES=`/`COLUMNS=` exported *empty* makes the game state a falsehood about the terminal (actionable; answers your question)

You asked whether the guard should check for empty values. It should. **ncurses ignores any `LINES`/`COLUMNS` that does not parse to a positive integer**, so the guard's protective rationale does not apply to those values — measured in a pane grown 100x30 → 110x34, ncurses 6.6.20251231:

| exported | `LINES`/`COLS` after `initscr()` | after the pane grew |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` | 20x70 (env honoured) | **still 20x70** — pinned, `is_term_resized(LINES,COLS)=0` |
| `LINES=` `COLUMNS=` | 30x100 (terminal) | 34x110 — **tracking normally** |
| `LINES=abc` / `LINES=0` | 30x100 (terminal) | 34x110 — **tracking normally** |

So with `LINES= COLUMNS=` exported the guard suppresses the ioctl where there was nothing to protect. End-to-end, on a real 100x30 terminal (started 70x20, grown before answering yes), `./build/ci-debug/sst -t`:

```
Terminal too small (need 72x24) -- using classic display.
Terminal is 70x20 -- need 72x24, staying classic.     <- terminal is really 100x30
```

The panels never come back although the terminal fits and ncurses is tracking it, and the new notice tells the player a size their terminal has not been for a while. `main` cannot print this line at all, so the misstatement is new with this change. The precise fix is to mirror ncurses' own rule (`_nc_getenv_num`: set **and** parses wholly to a value > 0), not merely non-empty — `LINES=0` and `LINES=abc` are in the same bucket. Low frequency, one condition to fix; your call, but "unset" is the wrong test.

You went beyond `code-review`'s proposal so the broken configuration is unreachable "one play-again later". Nothing pins that. I built the rejected alternative on a copy outside the repository (`ncalls > 1 || getenv(...) == NULL`, i.e. the guard on the first call only) and:

## Verdict

**Request changes.** Reviewed the worktree at `HEAD = 91fbe91` (branch `feat/tui-retry-per-game`, no commits): unstaged changes to `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/sst.c`, `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `tests/tui.sh`, `sst.doc`, `README.md`. No staged or untracked content. Two things stand between this and approval: one process gap you did not speak to, and one behavioral hole in `size_pinned()` that I reproduced against the binary in `build/debug`.

Everything I checked from the earlier rounds is answered. `size_pinned()` is now the single predicate on both sides; the `env size:` arm's `unwanted` is anchored (see below); the three column-width claims in the notices are right (I counted: 57, 57, 49 at two-digit sizes); `proutf` + `skip(1)` is correct against `sst.c:934-954`; CRLF is preserved in `sst.doc`; `getenv`/`strtol` are declared via `sst.h`'s `<stdlib.h>`; both readers do loop on `KEY_RESIZE` (`tui.c:1325`, `tui.c:1421`); and the retry cannot fire on a non-size refusal because `refusedlines` stays 0.

## Findings

### Blocker

**1. No claim about `ui-review`, on a diff that plainly reaches the player.** (process; `sst.c:493-494`, `sst.c:564-565`)

You told me `code-review` history and that `verifier` ran (PASS, two findings, one running concurrently over this state). You said nothing about `ui-review` — not that it ran, not on which state, not why it was skipped. `.claude/agents/code-review.md:48-62` makes that unanswered rather than answered in your favor, and the diff is not arguable: it reworded a startup notice a player reads (`It stays classic: restart sst at 72x24...` → `Grow the terminal to 72x24 and the next game gets panels.`), added a new line the player reads at the play-again boundary (`Terminal is 80x22 -- need 72x24, staying classic.`), and makes the panels appear mid-session where they previously never could.

It also matters *which* state: this round's predicate change is itself player-visible. Under `LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` the previous state printed `Terminal is 100x30 -- ...` every game; this one prints nothing. That is a screen a `ui-review` from round six never saw.

Fix: state the last `ui-review` round's verdict and the journeys it says it exercised, and whether it saw this state. If it did not see this state, run it before committing — the rerun rule in AGENTS.md step 6 is exactly about fixes made after a pass reported.

### Should-fix

**2. `size_pinned()` treats *either* variable as pinning *both*, which silently disables the whole feature when only `COLUMNS` is exported — and the comments justifying it are measurably wrong.** (`tui.c:1000-1027`, used at `tui.c:1051` and `tui.c:1148`; comment at `tui.c:1126-1136`; test comment at `tests/tui.sh:2779-2785`)

You asked about this case; it is worse than the odd corner it looks like, because a pinned *width* is usually a correct width and only the *height* was ever the problem.

Measured on this worktree's `build/debug/sst`, pane 80x20 grown to 80x30 at the play-again prompt:

- no environment: second game comes up with panels (`lq Quadrant qqq...` at row 1) — the feature working;
- `COLUMNS=80` exported: second game is classic, and silent. No panels, no `staying classic` line, nothing.

`COLUMNS=80` is a common thing to have exported (Docker images, CI, a `.bashrc` that exports it). And note the asymmetry it creates: with `COLUMNS=80` and a terminal that is *already* 80x30, `tui_init()`'s first call brings the panels up quite happily. The retry path is stricter than the startup path has ever been, for the same environment.

The comments assert the opposite, in the strongest form. `tui.c:1026` — "where it is TRUE, the size the game runs on cannot change" — and `tui.c:1128-1130` — "having done so it stops tracking the terminal at all, so `sync_size()` returns early for the rest of the session". Against ncurses 6.6.20251231, the version the comment cites, in a pane grown 70x20 → 100x30 with a live handler:

```
env COLUMNS=100:  start LINES=20 COLS=100 -> getch=410 (KEY_RESIZE) LINES=30 COLS=100
env LINES=20:     start LINES=20 COLS=70  -> getch=410 (KEY_RESIZE) LINES=20 COLS=100
env (both pinned):start LINES=20 COLS=70  -> getch=410 (KEY_RESIZE) LINES=20 COLS=70
```

ncurses honours the two independently; the free dimension keeps tracking and keeps delivering `KEY_RESIZE`. Your both-pinned measurement is correct; the generalization from it is what the gate actually runs on, and that is the part that is false. This is the "reachability wrong" shape AGENTS.md collects in #156.

Fix, either way but not neither:

- Per-variable, which makes the retry match startup and costs a few lines — `static int pinned(const char *name)`, then `resize_term(pinned("LINES") ? LINES : winsz.ws_row, pinned("COLUMNS") ? COLS : winsz.ws_col)` and, in `tui_size_changed_since_refusal()`, `if (!pinned("LINES") && ws.ws_row != refusedlines) return TRUE;` and the mirror for columns. Both-pinned then falls out unchanged, so the `env size:` arm still holds, and the `static const char *const` array you asked about disappears with it.
- Or keep the over-approximation deliberately and say so in all three comments: that either variable is taken to pin both, that the free dimension does in fact keep tracking (with this measurement), and that the cost is a player with `COLUMNS` exported who grows the height getting classic in silence. Then it is a documented trade rather than a claim a reader will believe.

### Nit

**3. The parse diverges from `_nc_getenv_num` in three ways, while the comment says it is that rule.** (`tui.c:1002-1006`, `tui.c:1021-1023`)

`_nc_getenv_num` uses `strtol(src, &dst, 0)` and rejects on `(int)value < value`. Measured against ncurses 6.6.20251231 at a 70x20 pane:

```
LINES=0x50                  -> ncurses: LINES=80  (honoured)   size_pinned(): not pinned
LINES=99999999999999999999  -> ncurses: LINES=20  (ignored)    size_pinned(): pinned
LINES=030                   -> ncurses: LINES=24  (octal)      size_pinned(): pinned (same verdict)
LINES=+30, " 30", 30abc, -5 -> agree
```

So `LINES=0x50` makes the ioctl override a size somebody pinned on purpose — the exact harm the guard exists to prevent — and an overflowing or `>INT_MAX` value disables the retry for a size ncurses ignored. Both are pathological values and neither is worth a finding on its own; what makes it worth an edit is that the comment states this *is* ncurses' rule. Two tokens settle it: `strtol(v, &end, 0)` and `n > 0 && (int)n == n`. If you would rather not mirror it, drop "The rule is ncurses' own" and say it is a deliberately simpler base-10 test.

## On your two open questions

- **Nit 4 (the `unchanged:` arm's `unwanted` going vacuous)** — your resolution holds, and by a wider margin than you credited it with. I ran that journey at 70x20: the notice, when it prints, lands immediately before `Would you like a regular, tournament, or frozen game?` with nothing between them (`sst.c:566` `skip(1)`, then straight into `setup()`), and the arm waits for that very string. Vacuity would take ~18 lines appearing between the two. I would not spend anything more on it. The `env size:` arm's `unwanted` is anchored differently and just as well: the `screen | grep -qF 'play again'` check above it proves text from *before* the retry is still visible, and anything the retry printed would be below it.
- **Whether the second reversal left anything stale** — `README.md`, `sst.doc` and the `sst.c:469-492` notice comment all agree with the code, the two survivors of `grep` for the old "once at startup" claim are unrelated (`tui.c:1080`, `tests/tui.sh:2861`, both about SIGWINCH), and the test comments name the mutation that proved each new assertion. The only stale text I found is the pair in finding 2.

## Not reviewed

- I did not build, run `ctest`, or run `tests/tui.sh`; that is the `verifier`'s pass and it is running over this state. My reproductions used the existing `build/debug/sst` (mtime 01:01:42, newer than `tui.c`, so current) on private tmux sockets (`-L cr1/cr2/cr3/crv`), from a scratch directory, killed on the same sockets.
- I did not re-derive the leak or the `tui_init()`-called-twice analysis you carried forward; you said they were taken as read and I found nothing new against them.
- #162 and #163 are outside this slice and correctly filed rather than fixed. The new comment at `tests/tui.sh:2780-2781` describes `is_term_resized()` correctly for the pinned case, so it does not reintroduce #163.

 *
 * The rule is ncurses' own, from _nc_getenv_num: strtol with base 0, so
 * 0x50 and 030 count, and the result must be above zero and fit an int.
 * Everything else -- unset, empty, 0, negative, trailing rubbish, or too
 * large -- ncurses ignores, taking the terminal instead. Measured
 * against ncurses 6.6.20251231 at a 70x20 pane: LINES=0x50 gives 80,
 * LINES=030 gives 24, LINES=99999999999999999999 is ignored. Testing

 * would stand the panels down where nothing was pinned at all.

 * Asked per variable because ncurses honours them per variable. With
 * LINES=20 alone, in a pane grown from 70x20 to 100x30, curses reports
 * 20x100 and still delivers KEY_RESIZE: the pinned dimension stays put
 * and the free one follows. Taking either to pin both would stand the
 * retry down for anyone with COLUMNS exported -- Docker images, CI
 * runners and shell profiles all do it -- on a terminal whose height
 * was the only thing ever wrong.
 *
 * Both places that reason about size ask this, and for the same reason:
 * a pinned dimension cannot change, so it must neither be overridden
 * nor counted as having moved. */
static int pinned(const char *name) {
	const char *v = getenv(name);
	char *end;
	long n;

	if (v == NULL || *v == '\\0') return FALSE;
	n = strtol(v, &end, 0);
	return *end == '\\0' && n > 0 && (int)n == n;
}
'''

	    winsz.ws_row > 0 && winsz.ws_col > 0)
		resize_term(pinned("LINES") ? LINES : winsz.ws_row,
			    pinned("COLUMNS") ? COLS : winsz.ws_col);"""
s = s.replace(old2, new2)

	   the refusal from curses, the answer from the terminal -- and a
	   pinned size holds them apart for good: curses reports what was
	   exported, the ioctl reports the window. They could never agree,
	   so this said the terminal had moved on every game, and the

	   terminal had moved on every game and the caller quoted a size

	   terminal's, and the ws_row/ws_col guard leaves the whole call

Fourth round on branch `feat/tui-retry-per-game` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek (no commits; unstaged in `sst.c`, `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `tests/tui.sh`, `sst.doc`, `README.md`). Read AGENTS.md and .claude/agents/ui-review.md.

**You are owed this round and `code-review` called me on not offering it.** Your round 3 verdict was acceptable-as-is, but three rounds of fixes have happened since, and one of them changes what a player sees in a configuration you have never been shown.

## What has changed since your round 3

**The ioctl I added to defeat curses' cached size was overriding an exported `LINES`/`COLUMNS`, which ncurses honours.** `code-review` found the consequence: ncurses, having taken a dimension from the environment, stops tracking the terminal on it, so `sync_size()` returns early forever. The panels came up and then **froze at their startup size**, the frame breaking rather than clipping on the first resize. That contradicted `README.md`'s "Resizing the terminal is fine at any point" and the clipping promise below it. Your round 2 had confirmed the override as an improvement, on the strength of a corrupted grid it fixed; nobody looked at what happened afterwards.

It took two more attempts to get right, and both intermediate states were player-visible:

1. First fix: skip the ioctl when either variable is set. This left a worse bug — `tui_size_changed_since_refusal()` still read the terminal while the recorded refusal came from curses, so with the size pinned the two could never agree and the game printed `Terminal is 70x20 -- need 72x24, staying classic.` **every game**, quoting a size that was not the player's window, to a player who had touched nothing.
2. Current fix: one predicate, `pinned(name)`, asked **per variable** by both sides. A pinned dimension is neither overridden nor counted as having moved; a free one takes the terminal's size. It uses ncurses' own parse rule (`_nc_getenv_num`): base 0, above zero, fits an int — so `LINES=`, `LINES=0`, `LINES=abc` are ignored and `LINES=0x50` is honoured as 80. I measured all of those directly.

**What this means for you:** with any dimension pinned, the game should now behave exactly as `main` does — no override, no notice, no new screen. With `COLUMNS` alone pinned (common: Docker images, CI runners, shell profiles export it), the retry should still work, because only the height was ever wrong.

## What to check

- **`env COLUMNS=80` alone**, terminal 80x20 grown to 80x30 between games: the panels should come back for the second game and nothing should be said. This is the case the change nearly broke silently, and the one most likely to be real.
- **`env LINES=20 COLUMNS=70`** in a 100x30 terminal, played across two or three games with no resize: classic throughout, and **silence** — no `staying classic` line, ever. Compare against a `main` build; they should be indistinguishable.
- **`env LINES= COLUMNS=`** (both exported empty): should behave as if unset — panels refused at 70x20, and back after growing to 100x30.
- That nothing in the ordinary no-environment path regressed from what you approved in round 3: the two-line startup notice, the `Terminal is NxM -- need 72x24, staying classic.` diagnostic at 80x22, silence when nothing moved, and the panels coming back and following a later resize.
- `README.md:94-113` and `sst.doc:1547-1563`, which no longer mention `LINES`/`COLUMNS` at all — the sentence claiming the terminal is asked rather than the environment was deleted when it stopped being true. Is that silence right, or does a player who pins a dimension and gets no panels deserve a word?

Same constraints: private tmux socket via `-L <yourname>` with `-f /dev/null`, never a bare `kill-server`, never `kill-session` on a session you did not create, scratch directory with a copy of `sst.doc`, never redirect the game's stdout in the pane.

Read-only: report findings, never edit.

content.text:
## Verdict

Acceptable as-is, with one small documentation finding I'd like answered. The three cases the brief singled out all behave correctly on the current state: `COLUMNS=80` alone at 80x20 grown to 80x30 brings the panels back for the second game and says nothing; `LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` in a 100x30 window plays three games classic and is byte-identical to a `main` build except for the intended second notice line and the random galaxy; `LINES= COLUMNS=` empty behaves exactly as unset. The no-environment path is unchanged from what I approved in round 3 — two-line startup notice, silence when nothing moved, `Terminal is 80x22 -- need 72x24, staying classic.` when the player grew and missed, and the panels coming back at 72x24 and afterwards *following* resizes (grow to 100x30, clip at 68x18, restore at 80x24), which is the freeze `code-review` found and it is genuinely gone. The one thing I'd still push on is the doc silence: with a dimension pinned the game can now print a size that is not the player's window, tell them to grow a terminal that is already large enough, and offer no route to the cause.

## Findings

**1. should-fix — `README.md:94-113` / `sst.doc:1547-1563`: nothing tells a player that an exported `LINES`/`COLUMNS` is what they are fighting.**

What a player experiences, measured: `env LINES=20 ./sst -t` in a **100x30** terminal prints

```
Terminal too small (need 72x24) -- using classic display.
Grow the terminal to 72x24 and the next game gets panels.
```

— on a window that is already 30 rows tall. They do as asked, grow it to 120x40, answer yes, and get

```
Terminal is 120x20 -- need 72x24, staying classic.
```

on a terminal that is 120 by **40**. Both of those lines are new or newly-worded on this branch, and the second is emitted by this change's own code, so this is a finding about the change and not about pre-existing ncurses behaviour (which is what makes the game trust the variable in the first place — `main` behaves identically in that respect; I diffed a `COLUMNS=100`-in-a-72-column start and the garbled shape is character-for-character the same). What the branch adds is an instruction that cannot be obeyed and a number that contradicts the player's own window, with the docs now saying nothing about where either comes from. The README already spends a clause on the tmux status bar for exactly this purpose — explaining a surprising number — and this is the other way to get one.

Concrete suggestion, one clause in each. README, after "…a tmux status bar can cost you the row that decides it.":

> If the size it names is not your window's, something in your environment has exported `LINES` or `COLUMNS`; ncurses believes those over the terminal, and no amount of resizing will change them. Unset them and start again.

and the same in `sst.doc` at ~68 columns with CRLF, to match the paragraph it joins. (A code-side alternative — naming the environment in the diagnostic when the ioctl and curses disagree — is more machinery than the problem is worth; the sentence is enough.)

**2. nit — `sst.c:566` (`tui_shutdown()` before the farewell): after a successful retry, the restored screen leaves a stale answer above the goodbye.**

Only reachable on this branch's new path (classic first game, panels from the second). Quitting for good restores the normal screen, which still holds the *first* game's conversation, so the last two lines a player sees are:

```
Do you want to play again?y

May the Great Bird of the Galaxy roost upon your home planet.
```

They answered `n`; the screen says `y`. Harmless and inherent to the alternate screen — when the panels come up at startup the normal screen holds only a shell prompt, so it has never shown before. Reporting it for the record; I would not change anything for it.

## What I exercised

Built `debug` from the branch and a pristine `main` (`git archive main` into a scratch tree, own `build/`) for comparison. All TUI work through `tmux -f /dev/null -L uir4`, session `uir4s`, cleaned up with `kill-server` on that socket only; game run from a scratch working dir so `.trk` files landed there; stdout never redirected in the pane.

- **`COLUMNS=80` alone**, 80x20 → panels refused, notice correct → quit/score/no → grow to 80x30 → `y`: panels came up, no `staying classic`, second game reached its prompt with both panels populated. Then, panels up, **grew height to 80x40 and shrank to 80x18** — the free dimension follows and the panels clip correctly; widening to 110 leaves them at 80, which is ncurses honouring the pin and identical on `main`.
- **`LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` in 100x30**, three consecutive games, no resize: classic throughout, zero occurrences of `staying classic`; full scrollback diffed against the same run on `main` — the only differences are the intended second-line rewording and the random galaxy.
- **`LINES= COLUMNS=`** (both exported empty), 70x20 → refused → grown to 100x30 → panels back, silent, populated.
- **`LINES=20` alone in 100x30 grown to 120x40** — the case in finding 1.
- **No environment**: 70x20 startup notice (both lines); second game with no resize → silence; third game after growing to 80x22 → `Terminal is 80x22 -- need 72x24, staying classic.` on its own line ahead of the first setup question; retry to exactly **72x24** → panels, then 100x30, 68x18 (clipped, `>` truncation intact), back to 80x24; `chart` in the retried session pages correctly at 72x24; ordinary 80x24 panels-from-startup journey unaffected; exit path farewell survives the screen restore.
- **`TERM=dumb`** at 100x30 across two games with a resize between: single-line notice, no "grow the terminal" line, no `staying classic` ever.
- **Piped journeys**, branch vs `main`, both plain and `-t`, using `tournament 7 short novice pw` for a deterministic first game: identical for the whole deterministic portion; piped `-t` prints only `Full-screen mode needs a terminal -- using the classic display.` and never the growth advice or the diagnostic.
- Read the full branch diff (`sst.c`, `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `tests/tui.sh`, `README.md`, `sst.doc`), checked the edited `sst.doc` lines keep CRLF and stay inside ~68 columns, and confirmed `main` never mentioned `LINES`/`COLUMNS` either.
- Chased one apparent regression to ground: a run where `y` at the play-again prompt appeared to end the game. It was my harness matching a stale `play again` in the scrollback — the second game's `quit` goes straight to the play-again question without asking about the score, so my `n` answered it. Reproduced identically on `main`; not a branch behaviour.

# Super Star Trek

Super Star Trek is an old text-only game, an early example of a turn-based space strategy sim, written in BASIC. In this game, you are the captain of the starship Enterprise, and your mission is to scout the federation space and eliminate all the invading Klingon ships. You will have to manage the ship energy carefully, use phasers and torpedoes to destroy the Klingons, and find starbases to repair damages and replenish your energy. All of this, rendered with a few characters on screen and a lot of imagination.

Super Star Trek is probably the most famous early text-only game ever created and it inspired many other videogames. Since the code was public domain, during the years, it was changed and improved many times. There are literally thousands of versions out there. All of them are nice, but my preference goes to the classic 1978 version called Super Star Trek.

[Read more about Star Trek and Super Star Trek.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek_%281971_video_game%29)

### Full-screen mode

Run `sst -t` for a full-screen interface: the short-range scan and the
ship's status stay on screen in two panels while the usual game
conversation scrolls below them. It needs a terminal of at least 72x24
(columns by rows) and can be combined with the fixed-coordinate option
(`sst -f -t`).
Without `-t` the game uses its classic scrolling display.

Resizing the terminal is fine at any point. The display follows it
straight away — while the game is waiting for you to answer, and while
it is waiting for a keystroke at a pause — and both the question you
were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so
long as there is still room for them. Older text that no longer fits
scrolls away, as it would in any terminal.

Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for, they clip rather
than rearrange themselves. A line with more to show than there is room
for ends in `>`, so a shortened number is never mistaken for a small
one, and a heading with no room left is dropped rather than shortened.
A terminal too short for the panels is the panels' problem, not the
conversation's: they lose rows off the bottom, the grid keeping its
numbering for as long as it has rows to number, and the conversation
keeps three rows down to six — two of it and the line the prompt or the
pager sits on. Below six there is not that much left to divide and it
keeps what there is: two rows at five and one at four. So the prompt
stays on screen down to four rows, and down to six a paged command shows
a line of itself before stopping to ask — at five its one line goes to
the blank that `lrscan`, `chart` and `status` open with, though
`srscan`, which has none, still shows a line there, and at four the
pager takes the only row and a paged command shows nothing of itself at
all. Shorter than four the panels have taken the screen: the game still
reads what you type, with nothing on it to say so.

Growing the terminal back brings the panels with it, however far the
squeeze went: they redraw from the game state, so they return full of
live readings. The conversation cannot be rebuilt that way — curses
does not reflow it — so whatever scrolled away while the window was
small is gone for good, and an older line that was cut short stays cut
short. Every reading is a command away, though, and none of them costs
anything: `srscan`, `status`, `chart`, `damages`.

The line you are on usually comes back, and it is the one that matters:
a question or a pause the game was part way through writing is written
out again whole once there is room for it, so you are not left typing
into the tail of a prompt. A few prompts finish their line before they
stop to wait; those come back too, with the answer going on the row
below the question — or after it, where the window is down to its last
row.
Only their final line comes back, so a question asked over several
lines returns as the last of them. An answer you had already started
typing usually comes back with its question, on the row below it. You
may get back only one of them. Where the question ended its own line the
two sit on separate rows, so a wrapped answer needs three rows and a
window of one or two — five rows or fewer — cannot hold the pair; a
question that has itself wrapped needs a row more again. The question is
what goes, leaving your own typing with nothing above it to say what it
answers, and on a very wide terminal it is the answer that goes instead,
however tall the window is. Shorter still and only part of whichever
survived is left, and sometimes neither comes back, leaving older
conversation on screen with the game waiting behind it.

When the question and everything you typed are both on screen, carry on
and answer — that is the ordinary case now. When they are not, give the
terminal another row or two first: that usually brings it back with
your typing untouched, which beats retyping it. A very wide terminal is
the exception — more rows will not bring the answer back there, though
making it narrow enough will.

If it does not come back, or the terminal cannot grow, do not just
answer it, and do not press Enter either: whatever you typed is still
in the buffer, and a yes/no question reads the *first* letter, so an
`N` typed after a `y` you cannot see answers yes.
Press Ctrl-U first, which throws the line away, and then answer. What
you type lands on whatever the window happens to be showing; the line
it fell on clears when you press Enter, though the characters you
typed stay where they landed.

If the prompt is missing or cut off and you had not started answering
it, press Enter. Nothing waiting behind one commits you to anything
then: a pause moves on, the self-destruct password reads the empty
answer as a refusal and stands the sequence down, and a yes/no
question comes back only as `Please answer with "Y" or "N":`, without
saying again what it asked — answer `N` there and you are back at the
prompt, free to give the command again.

If full-screen mode isn't possible — the terminal is too small, the
game isn't attached to one (piped input, redirected output, a job with
no tty), or `TERM` names a terminal that can't address the cursor —
`-t` prints a notice and plays in the classic display instead. That
game stays classic to the end — enlarging the window will not bring the
panels up part way through it.

A game that went classic gets the choice made again for the next one,
though. So if the terminal was too small and you have since made it
bigger, answering yes to "Do you want to play again?" starts the next
game with the panels. If you resized it and it is still too small, the
game says what size it read back rather than leaving you to wonder —
72x24 is the whole of what it takes, and a tmux status bar can cost you
the row that decides it. Leave the terminal alone and it stays quiet:
you were told at startup and nothing has changed since.

The build is CMake, driven through presets:

```sh
cmake --preset debug           # or release
cmake --build --preset debug
./build/debug/sst
```

You need a C17 compiler, CMake 3.21 or newer, and ncurses

`ctest --preset debug` runs the test suite, which includes a full-screen

that one test reports as skipped.

`cmake --list-presets` shows them all. There are four: `debug` and
`release`, and `ci-debug` and `ci-release`, which add `-Werror` and are
exactly what CI runs — so you can reproduce a CI warning locally rather
than discovering it in a pull request.

## Verdict

**Request changes.** Two should-fix findings, one nit. No blockers.

Reviewed state: worktree on `feat/tui-retry-per-game`, no commits (`HEAD` = `main` = `91fbe91`), unstaged changes only, in `sst.c`, `tui.c`, `tui.h`, `tests/tui.sh`, `sst.doc`, `README.md`. Nothing staged, nothing untracked.

### Review coverage — satisfied

The diff plainly reaches the player (two reworded notices, one new one, and a retry that can swap the whole display mid-session). The `ui-review` round 4 claim you gave names configurations that map onto the diff's actual surface: the `pinned()` per-variable rewrite (`COLUMNS=80` alone, `LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` both, `LINES= COLUMNS=` empty) and the no-environment retry path including panels following a later resize. That is the delta round 3 did not see, and the earlier rounds account for the notice text and the `skip(1)`. I take the pass as having run on this state. My findings below are things it could not have seen from the screens it drove — see should-fix 2 for the one configuration none of the four rounds covered.

### What I checked directly

- `pinned()` against ncurses' real rule. I compiled your predicate side by side with `_nc_getenv_num` (installed ncurses is 6.6.20251231, matching the comment) over 18 inputs including `""`, `0`, `-5`, `20abc`, `" 20"`, `"\t8"`, `+20`, `0x50`, `030`, `0x0`, `2147483647`, `2147483648`, `4294967301`, `99999999999999999999`. **Zero mismatches.** On your three specific questions: the `(int)n == n` test is exactly equivalent to ncurses' `(int)value < value` for `n > 0`, since any `n > INT_MAX` has `(int)n <= INT_MAX < n`; `errno`/`ERANGE` needs no check because `strtol` returns `LONG_MAX` on overflow and `(int)n == n` rejects it on LP64, while on ILP32 `long == int` and ncurses accepts it too — so you track ncurses either way, which is the property that matters; and base 0 has no downside I can find, because it is what ncurses uses.
- The two call sites. `resize_term(rows, cols)` argument order is right. Mixing curses' cached value for a pinned dimension with the ioctl for a free one is correct as written: on the first call the pinned value *is* what `initscr()` just derived from the same variable, and on a retry `initscr()` is a no-op (`_nc_globals.init_screen` guard), so `LINES`/`COLS` still hold the pinned value while the free dimension is stale — exactly the split the code makes. `tui_refused_size()` is read after `tui_init()`, so the quoted size is the refreshed one. `resized` is computed before, so it measures the player's action. The `!tui_init() && resized` short-circuit still calls `tui_init()` unconditionally.
- SIGWINCH ledger across refuse → retry → refuse → retry-success: `oldwinch` is re-read per call and on a retry equals what the previous give-up restored, so no handler leaks into the classic path; `cursewinch` is captured once and reinstalled only past the size gate. Correct.
- No double `atexit(tui_shutdown)` — a failed retry returns before it, and a successful one can happen at most once because `sst.c` guards on `!tui_active`.
- Pager state at the retry point: `ja()` → `scan()` sets `linecount = 0`, so a successful retry cannot open the second game with a spurious `[HIT SPACE BAR]`. `tui_ingame` is FALSE by then (`finish.c:72`), so the comment at `sst.c:542` holds.
- Piped `-t` (golden/journey/eof) is untouched: `stdio_is_terminal()` fails first, `refusedlines` stays 0, nothing prints. `tests/journey.sh:161`'s `"classic display"` match still holds.
- Both TUs compile clean under `-std=gnu17 -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror`, at `-O2` (Release shape) and `-O0 -DDEBUG` (Debug shape).
- No stale text: nothing anywhere still greps for or repeats `It stays classic: restart sst at 72x24`; sst.doc's CRLF is preserved on every added line; all `sst.doc:NNN` citations in the tree are below 1546, so the insertion moves none of them.

## Findings

### Should-fix 1 — `tests/tui.sh:32` (and the whole file): an exported `LINES`/`COLUMNS` in the environment running the suite reaches the game, and the new assertions then fail

`tmux` passes the client environment straight through to the pane's command; I confirmed it (`LINES=99 COLUMNS=190` exported → `printenv` inside a 70x20 pane prints `99` and `190`). Nothing in `tests/tui.sh` neutralises them.

```
$ env COLUMNS=190 tmux ... new-session -d -x 70 -y 20 ...   # then quit, n, resize 80x22, y
Terminal too small (need 72x24) -- using classic display.
Terminal is 190x22 -- need 72x24, staying classic.

No failures, deterministic or flaky. Everything the brief asked about checks out; two non-blocking notes below.

---

### 1. `pinned()` vs ncurses — all four dimensions, measured

System ncurses is **6.6.20251231** (`ncurses6-config --version`), exactly the version the comments in `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tui.c` cite. I built a probe that links real ncurses, calls `initscr()` and reports `LINES`/`COLS`, alongside a verbatim copy of `pinned()`, and ran it in a **70x20** tmux pane (own socket, `-f /dev/null`) across 16 cases. `pinned()` agreed with ncurses in **every one** — TRUE exactly when curses' value diverged from the pane:

| `LINES` | curses (cols x rows) | `pinned("LINES")` | agree |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| unset | 70x20 | 0 | ✓ |
| `0x50` | 70x**80** | 1 | ✓ base 0 |
| `030` | 70x**24** | 1 | ✓ base 0 (octal) |
| `+30` | 70x**30** | 1 | ✓ |
| `  30` (leading spaces) | 70x**30** | 1 | ✓ |
| `25` | 70x**25** | 1 | ✓ |
| `99999999999999999999` | 70x20 | 0 | ✓ int bound |
| `2147483648` (INT_MAX+1) | 70x20 | 0 | ✓ int bound |
| `` (empty) / `0` / `abc` / `-5` / `30x` | 70x20 | 0 | ✓ ignored forms |

Per-variable independence, all three shapes: `COLUMNS=88` alone → `88x20`, pinnedLINES=0/pinnedCOLUMNS=1; `LINES=25 COLUMNS=88` → `88x25`, 1/1; **`LINES= COLUMNS=88` → `88x20`, 0/1** — the exact shape the new `one pinned:` case exports. The three numbers the comment states (`0x50`→80, `030`→24, huge→ignored, at 70x20) reproduce verbatim.

### 2. `(int)n == n` — right test, not UB

Not undefined behaviour: converting an out-of-range value to a signed integer type is **implementation-defined** (C17 6.3.1.3p3), and GCC/Clang document two's-complement truncation. Crucially it mirrors ncurses' own `(int) value < value` in `_nc_getenv_num` **bug for bug**:

- LP64 (here): `strtol("999…") == LONG_MAX` with `ERANGE`; `(int)LONG_MAX == -1 != LONG_MAX` → FALSE. ncurses: `-1 < LONG_MAX` → rejected. Same answer, confirmed empirically above.
- ILP32: `LONG_MAX == INT_MAX`, so both `pinned()` and ncurses accept the saturated value. Still the same answer — no divergence on any platform. Not checking `errno` is therefore correct, because ncurses does not check it either, and agreement with ncurses is the whole specification.

For positive `n`, `(int)n > n` is impossible, so `!=` and ncurses' `<` are equivalent. The test is right.

### 3. Builds

```
cmake --preset ci-debug   && cmake --build --preset ci-debug --clean-first
cmake --preset ci-release && cmake --build --preset ci-release --clean-first

- `ctest --preset ci-debug` — **11/11 passed**, 312.64 s (`tui` 167.45 s, `golden` 43.33 s, `help`, `instructions`, `score` all green).
- `ctest --preset ci-release` — **11/11 passed**, 304.20 s (`tui` 158.63 s).

`tests/tui.sh` ends with `printf 'tui OK\n'` after the last block and every earlier `exit` is a failure path, so a pass proves the three new blocks (`env size:`, `one pinned:`, `half grown:`/`unchanged:`) actually ran, in both configurations.

**The new `one pinned:` case is sound and discriminating.** Traced against the code: at 80x20 with `LINES= COLUMNS=80`, ncurses ignores the empty `LINES` and takes 20 rows → refusal at 20x80; grow to 80x30 → `tui_size_changed_since_refusal()` skips the pinned width, sees 30≠20 → TRUE; retry takes `ws_row=30` and keeps pinned `COLS=80` → panels. Under **either-pins-both** the retry keeps `LINES=20` and `want_quadtitle` fails; under **set-or-not** the empty `LINES` counts as pinned and it fails the same way. It cannot pass for a wrong reason — the panel title it asserts is drawn only in TUI mode and is matched on row 1 only.

### 5. Journeys (scripted tmux, own socket, `-f /dev/null`)

| Journey | Result |
| --- | --- |
| J1 70x20 → 100x30, second game | notice both lines, no `staying classic`, **panels**, farewell, clean exit |

**F1 — Missing coverage (the two rule dimensions no test exercises).** `tests/tui.sh` contains exactly two env-size cases: `env LINES=20 COLUMNS=70` (line 2795) and `env LINES= COLUMNS=80` (line 3292).
