the only guard, and the mutation showed three existing checks catch it
too. The comment says so now.

- **#168** — a *tolerated* pin still lets the panels overflow when the
  window shrinks under them; `resized()` cannot see it, since ncurses
  re-pins on every SIGWINCH. A resize-path fix, not a gate fix.
- **#169** — resizing the pinned axis between games gets no notice,
  because the check skips that axis. Named in a comment beside the skip.

content.content:
1ff91fe fix(tui): refuse a pinned size the terminal cannot draw (#170)
chore/static-analysis
## Problem

`.claude/agents/verifier.md` step 2 asks for static analysis:

> If `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, or `scan-build` is installed, run it over
> the changed files; if none is installed, report that as an environment
> gap rather than silently skipping.

The conditional is doing all the work. None of the three is installed on
the development machine, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` installs only
`libncurses-dev` and `tmux` — so **no static analyser runs anywhere in
this project**, on any machine, ever. The `verifier` reports the gap
honestly every time, exactly as instructed, and the gap never closes.

Across the passes on #90, #125 and #118 (PRs #142, #143, #144) that
report appeared in every single `verifier` run.

## Why it matters

The brief is written as though this leg of verification exists. It does
not, and a reader of `verifier.md` would reasonably believe otherwise —
the honest per-run disclosure only reaches whoever read that run's
output, not the next person deciding whether the checks are adequate.

What actually covers C here is `-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes` with
`-Werror` under the `ci-*` presets, which is real but is a different
class of check: it finds what the compiler happens to diagnose while
compiling, not what a dedicated analyser looks for. `gcc -fanalyzer` has
been used as a substitute by hand in several passes, and is closer, but
nothing asks for it.

This is a file full of raw buffer arithmetic — `restore_curline()` alone
juggles `char[512]`/`char[2048]`/`char[256]` against terminal widths, and
recent work there turned on exactly those bounds — so it is the kind of
code an analyser earns its keep on.

## Suggested fix

Pick one and make it real, rather than leaving three conditional names:

- Install `cppcheck` in the CI workflow (one apt line on Linux; Homebrew
  has it for macOS) and run it over the `.c` files, failing on its
  error-level findings. Cheapest, and puts the check somewhere it cannot
  be skipped.
- Or, if a per-run analyser is not wanted, use `gcc -fanalyzer` — no
  install needed, already exercised by hand — and say so in
  `verifier.md` in place of the three conditional names.
- Either way, `verifier.md` should name the check the project actually
  has, so its step 2 describes something that runs.

## Where it was found

Reported by the `verifier` sub-agent in its "Environment issues" section
on every pass across three changes. Filed rather than fixed in any of
them, per AGENTS.md step 9 — it is about the project's checks rather
than about those changes.

Follow the workflow in [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).

#!/bin/sh
# Static analysis over the game's C sources.
#
# This is the check .claude/agents/verifier.md's step 2 asks for. It used
# to ask for cppcheck, clang-tidy or scan-build "if installed", and none
# of the three was installed on the development machine or in CI -- so
# the leg never ran anywhere, the verifier reported the gap honestly on
# every pass, and the gap stayed open. #147.
#
# GCC's own analyzer is what the project actually has: no install, and
# already the compiler CI builds with on Linux. It is a different check
# from the -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes the ci-* presets make
# fatal -- those are what the compiler notices while generating code,
# where this walks paths and tracks what has been written to.
#
# Usage: analyze.sh [build-type]
# Exits 77 (ctest SKIP_RETURN_CODE) where no analyzer-capable compiler
# is available, except on Linux CI, where it fails instead.

set -u

# The sources live beside this script's parent, and that is how the
# other tests here find what they read.
srcdir=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
config="${1:-Debug}"

# The flags CMakeLists.txt compiles with, less the ones that only affect
# code generation. -DDEBUG matters: without it the debug command and
# everything behind it is not compiled, so half of sst.c would go
# unanalysed in a Release run.
flags="-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING"
case "$config" in
	Debug|debug) flags="$flags -DDEBUG" ;;
esac

work=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT HUP INT TERM PIPE

# Find a compiler whose -fanalyzer is real. Asking the version string is
# not enough: macOS ships clang as `gcc`, which takes -fanalyzer only as
# far as an error. Compiling something is the question worth asking.
cc=""
for candidate in "${CC:-}" gcc gcc-15 gcc-14 gcc-13; do
	[ -n "$candidate" ] || continue
	command -v "$candidate" >/dev/null 2>&1 || continue
	if echo 'int main(void){return 0;}' > "$work/probe.c" &&
	   "$candidate" -fanalyzer -c -o "$work/probe.o" "$work/probe.c" \
	       >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		cc="$candidate"
		break
	fi
done

if [ -z "$cc" ]; then
	# Linux CI builds with GCC, so a skip there would mean the analyzer
	# had gone missing from the one place it is guaranteed. macOS CI
	# builds with clang and is expected to skip.
	if [ -n "${CI:-}" ] && [ "$(uname -s)" = Linux ]; then
		echo "FAIL: no compiler with -fanalyzer on Linux CI, so nothing was analysed" >&2
		exit 1
	fi
	echo "SKIP: no compiler with a working -fanalyzer" >&2
	exit 77
fi

# Prove the analyzer is live before believing a clean run.
#
# This is here because of how #147 came about. Several passes reported
# `gcc -fanalyzer -fsyntax-only` as clean; -fsyntax-only does not run
# the analyzer at all, so those runs were vacuous and looked exactly
# like a pass. A check that cannot fail is worse than no check, and the
# only way to know this one can is to hand it something broken.
cat > "$work/canary.c" <<'EOF'
#include <stdlib.h>
int canary(void);
int canary(void) {
	int *p = malloc(sizeof(int));
	free(p);
	return *p;			/* use after free */
}
EOF
if ! "$cc" -fanalyzer -c -o "$work/canary.o" "$work/canary.c" 2>&1 |
     grep -q 'Wanalyzer-use-after-free'; then
	echo "FAIL: $cc -fanalyzer did not flag a use-after-free, so a clean" >&2
	echo "      run over the sources would mean nothing" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# osx.c is excluded: it is the file that cannot include sst.h, and it
# compiles only against the platform headers CMake gives it. Everything
# else is analysed exactly as the build compiles it.
status=0
for src in "$srcdir"/*.c; do
	out="$work/$(basename "$src").txt"
	"$cc" -fanalyzer $flags -c -o "$work/obj.o" "$src" 2>"$out" || status=1
	if grep -q 'Wanalyzer' "$out"; then
		echo "FAIL: $(basename "$src") has analyzer findings" >&2
		cat "$out" >&2
		status=1
	fi
done

if [ "$status" -ne 0 ]; then
	exit 1
fi

printf 'analyze OK (%s)\n' "$cc"

content.text: Found it — GCC reported it as plain `-Wuse-after-free`, not `-Wanalyzer-*`, and my grep only looked for the latter. The fix is to make *any* diagnostic fatal rather than pattern-match:

input.command:

cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='tests/analyze.sh'; s=open(p).read()
old = '''status=0
for src in "$srcdir"/*.c; do
	out="$work/$(basename "$src").txt"
	"$cc" -fanalyzer $flags -c -o "$work/obj.o" "$src" 2>"$out" || status=1
	if grep -q 'Wanalyzer' "$out"; then
		echo "FAIL: $(basename "$src") has analyzer findings" >&2
		cat "$out" >&2
		status=1
	fi
done'''
assert s.count(old)==1
new = '''# -Werror, so any diagnostic fails rather than a pattern deciding which
# count. Grepping for -Wanalyzer looked right and was not: a planted
# use-after-free in sst.c came back as plain -Wuse-after-free, which
# -Wall raises before the analyzer gets to it, and the run reported
# clean. The ci-* presets already make -Wall -Wextra fatal, so anything
# new that stops the compile here is either an analyzer finding or
# something those builds would have caught anyway.
status=0
for src in "$srcdir"/*.c; do
	out="$work/$(basename "$src").txt"
	if ! "$cc" -fanalyzer $flags -Werror -c -o "$work/obj.o" "$src" \\
	     2>"$out"; then
		echo "FAIL: $(basename "$src") did not analyse clean" >&2
		cat "$out" >&2
		status=1
	fi
done'''
open(p,'w').write(s.replace(old,new))
print("ok")
PYEOF
tests/analyze.sh Debug; echo "exit=$?"

content.text:
## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed the worktree at HEAD `1ff91fe` on `chore/static-analysis`, no commits: modified `.claude/agents/verifier.md`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `setup.c`; untracked `tests/analyze.sh`. I ran `ctest --test-dir build/ci-debug -R '^analyze$'` (passes, 15.5s), reproduced the skip path (exit 77) and the `CI=1` Linux fail path (exit 1), and confirmed the flags ctest actually passes: `-std=gnu17 -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror -DDEBUG -I/usr/include`.

Nothing here is wrong about the game's behavior; the findings are all in the new script and the claims around it. Three of them are should-fix, and the first one defeats the change's own purpose on the one platform the author says CI will settle.

### Review coverage

Satisfied, and I checked it against the diff rather than taking it. The only player-reachable line is `setup.c:670`, and `ui-review`'s stated coverage — 96 A/B games byte-identical against a `main` build, 35 of them showing a `C` on a scan, 123 instrumented promotions with 0 mismatches — is aimed exactly at that line rather than at journeys the change cannot reach. The edits made after that round were comment-only (`setup.c` has no other change), so per step 6 no rerun was owed. The `CMakeLists.txt` change registers a test and touches no feature flag, so it does not change what is compiled into the game and owes nothing here.

I verified the equivalence independently: inside `if (quadnum >= 100)`, `klhere = quadnum/100 >= 1`, the Klingon loop therefore ran at least once, and `kx[klhere]`/`ky[klhere]` hold the last `dropin`'s `ix`/`iy`. `klhere <= 9` (the block returns for `quadnum > 999`), well inside `kx[21]`/`ky[21]` (`sst.h:272-273`). No `Rand()` calls added or removed, which is why the A/B recordings can be byte-identical.

### Findings

**should-fix — `tests/analyze.sh:51`: bare `mktemp -d`, unchecked, makes the whole test a silent no-op on macOS.**
BSD `mktemp` (macOS) requires a template in the non-`-t` form; `mktemp -d` alone prints usage and exits 1. With no `set -e` and no status check, `work` becomes empty, `set -u` is satisfied, and every subsequent path is absolute: the probe writes `/probe.c`, fails for every candidate, and the script exits 77. ctest reports `Skipped` and the macOS job goes green — indistinguishable from the intended "clang-only machine skips", and precisely the #147 failure mode (a check that never ran, reported as fine) reproduced in the fix for it. It also makes the Homebrew-`gcc-N` question you want CI to answer unanswerable, because macOS will skip for an unrelated reason. `tests/tui.sh:104` already uses the portable form; suggest `work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/sst-analyze.XXXXXX") || exit 1` plus `[ -n "$work" ] || exit 1`. (I could not test on macOS; the consistency argument stands either way, and the unchecked status is a defect regardless of who is right about BSD `mktemp`.)

**should-fix — `tests/analyze.sh:52`: the signal traps do not exit, so the script resumes with its work directory deleted.**
Proved locally under `/bin/sh` (dash): a `trap 'rm -rf "$w"' TERM` handler runs and execution *continues*, after which the EXIT trap fires a second time. Here that means a Ctrl-C during `ctest -R analyze` removes `$work` and then the loop keeps compiling into a directory that no longer exists, printing `FAIL: <file>.c did not analyse clean` with a cascade of gcc errors for all 13 sources and exiting 1 — a fabricated analysis failure from an interrupt. `tests/tui.sh:111-124` documents this exact hazard and uses one trap per signal with an explicit `exit`; match it (`trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 130' INT`, `143` TERM, `129` HUP, `141` PIPE).

**should-fix — `tests/analyze.sh:97-102` and `CMakeLists.txt:144-147`: a compiler that passes the probe but fails the canary is fatal, with no fallback, and the macOS comment names only two of three outcomes.**
The probe loop tries `gcc` first, and on macOS `gcc` is Apple clang. If clang ever accepts and ignores `-fanalyzer` (today it errors, which is what makes the probe work), the loop stops there, the canary fails, and the test exits 1 — even though `gcc-15`/`gcc-14` were the next two candidates. Moving the canary compile inside the probe loop turns that into "this candidate cannot analyse, try the next", which is what the loop is for, and costs one extra compile per candidate.

On the deliberate macOS call you asked about: letting CI settle it is defensible, but "Either outcome is fine -- more coverage, or a skip" is the part I'd dispute. GitHub's `macos-latest` images ship Homebrew GCC on `PATH`, so the probe will find `gcc-15`/`gcc-14` rather than skip, and the third outcome is the likely one: Homebrew GCC compiling 13 sources against the macOS SDK under `-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror`, where a single GCC-on-Darwin-only warning (or an SDK header incompatibility after an Xcode bump) turns both macOS jobs red on a check whose analysis value Linux already delivered. Per AGENTS.md's rule that a comment stating what can and cannot happen is read as specification, either say the third outcome exists and that you will treat it by restricting the probe, or restrict it now (e.g. skip on `Darwin` unless an opt-in env var is set).

**nit — `tests/analyze.sh:58`: the hard-coded `gcc-15 gcc-14 gcc-13` list ages into a silent skip.**
On the day the only Homebrew GCC is `gcc-16`, macOS quietly reports `Skipped` again with nobody notified — the same invisible-non-execution shape as above. Consider probing `gcc-*` from `PATH`, or at least noting in the comment that the list needs bumping.

**nit — `tests/analyze.sh:104`, `CMakeLists.txt` comment, `verifier.md:32`: "every .c the build compiles" / "every source" is not true.**
The build also compiles `tests/test_tuifmt.c` and `tests/test_rules.c` (`CMakeLists.txt:51,57`), which this loop does not reach. Given AGENTS.md's insistence that a comment's claim carry its source and hold at its own location, say "every .c in the source root — the 13 the `sst` target links" instead.

**nit — `tests/analyze.sh:42-44` vs `CMakeLists.txt:11-16`: the unconditional `-Werror` quietly overrides the `SST_WERROR` policy.**
`CMakeLists.txt` states the policy that a contributor on an untried compiler "gets the warning and a working build"; after this change they get a working build and a failing `analyze` test from an ordinary `-Wall` warning, since `-Werror` is added whatever the preset says. The rationale for `-Werror` over grepping for `-Wanalyzer` (lines 108-114) is sound and I would not change the mechanism — but one sentence in the CMake comment acknowledging that `ctest --preset debug` is now warning-fatal for this one test would keep the two policy statements from contradicting each other.

**nit — `CMakeLists.txt:157`: `analyze_flags` omits `CMAKE_C_FLAGS_<CONFIG>`.**
The ci-release run therefore analyses unoptimised code and differs from the ci-debug run only by `-DDEBUG`. That is probably the right trade (`-O3` makes `-fanalyzer` slower and noisier, and there are no `assert`s in the tree to care about `-DNDEBUG`), but the comment's "the build's own flags" reads as if optimisation came along, and AGENTS.md specifically notes that some warnings need optimisation to appear. Worth one clause saying `-O`/`-g` are deliberately left out.

**nit — `README.md:147-149`: "without it that one test reports as skipped" is now one of two skippable tests.**
A macOS reader with no Homebrew GCC will see a second `Skipped` and have nothing to look it up against.

**nit — `setup.c:667-669`: "the decrement between them is inside it" reads as a contradiction.**
There is no decrement between `klhere = quadnum/100` and `if (quadnum >= 100)`; the decrement is after the test, inside the block. The intended reading (nothing between them changes `quadnum`) is right, but a reader has to reconstruct it. Something like "nothing between them touches `quadnum` — the only decrement is inside this block" says it in one pass. The rest of the comment checks out.

**nit — `.claude/agents/verifier.md:29-44`: the step does not say what a `Skipped` `analyze` means.**
Output item 4 covers it generically ("never report a skipped check as a pass"), but this is the step whose entire history is a leg that silently did not run; one sentence — a skip means no static analysis ran on this machine and is reported as an environment gap — closes it at the place the verifier will be reading.

### Could not review

- macOS behavior of `mktemp -d` with no template, and whether Homebrew GCC compiles this tree against the macOS SDK cleanly: no macOS here, and no clang installed to test the `-fanalyzer` probe against. Findings 1 and 3 are argued from the repository's own idiom and from the runner images rather than from a run.

`tests/analyze.sh` is now a ctest test running `gcc -fanalyzer` over every source, any diagnostic fatal via `-Werror`. It skips where no compiler offers `-fanalyzer` and fails rather than skipping on Linux CI — the tmux idiom from `tests/tui.sh`.

## What building it turned up

**`gcc -fanalyzer -fsyntax-only` analyses nothing.** Several `verifier` passes this session reported it as a clean substitute; it exits 0 on a blatant use-after-free where `-fanalyzer -c` catches it. So those were not weaker checks but no check, reported as clean. The script therefore compiles a deliberate use-after-free canary first and fails if the analyzer does not flag it. Recorded on #147 as a correction to its premise.

**cppcheck could not be verified here** — no root, and the extracted `.deb` will not start without a `std.cfg` that cannot be placed. Choosing it would have meant shipping a check nobody here could execute.

**One line of game code changed.** `setup.c`'s commander promotion was `quad[ix][iy] = IHC;`, flagged as a read of uninitialized `ix`. A false positive, but the line now names the same square as `quad[kx[klhere]][ky[klhere]]`.

## Passes

- **`ui-review`: acceptable as-is.** It instrumented 150 games — 123 promotions, 0 mismatches, `klhere` from 1 to 9 — and ran 96 A/B games against a `main` build, byte-identical, 35 of them showing a `C` on a scan. Its two nits were both about my comment's length and a claim that read false at its own location; both fixed.
- **`verifier`: FAIL, and it was right.** `SKIP_RETURN_CODE 77` was missing from the `add_test`, so the skip path was a failure — which macOS CI and any clang-only machine would have hit. **All three of my mutation proofs ran the script directly and structurally could not see it.** Fixed and proved through ctest: no analyzer-capable compiler on PATH reports `Skipped`; the same with `CI=1` reports `Failed`.
- It also found the script restated the build's compile recipe by hand and had **already drifted** — no `-std`, so it analysed as C23 while every preset compiled `gnu17`. AGENTS.md's presets note is explicit about a recipe in a sixth file. `CMakeLists.txt` now passes `-std=gnu${CMAKE_C_STANDARD} ${CMAKE_C_FLAGS}` plus the curses includes, and the script has no recipe of its own.
- `ctest` 12/12 in both `ci-*` presets; both build clean under `-Werror`.

## Please scrutinise

- **`tests/analyze.sh` as a shell script** — quoting, the `mktemp`/`trap` cleanup, `set -u` with the unset-variable reads, and the compiler-probe loop.
- **Whether `-Werror` over the build's own flags is right**, given the `ci-*` builds already make most of them fatal.
- **The `setup.c` equivalence and its comment.**
- **The `verifier.md` rewrite** — it now names the check that exists and tells the reader not to substitute a hand-rolled analyser run, with the `-fsyntax-only` history as the reason.
- **One thing I have deliberately left to CI:** macOS runners build with clang, but often carry a Homebrew `gcc-N` that the probe loop would find and use against the macOS SDK. Either outcome is acceptable — more coverage, or a skip — and I have said so in the `CMakeLists.txt` comment. Tell me if that is the wrong call.

## Verdict: request changes

Reviewed the worktree at HEAD `1ff91fe` on `chore/static-analysis`, no commits: modified `.claude/agents/verifier.md`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `setup.c`; untracked `tests/analyze.sh`. I ran `ctest --test-dir build/ci-debug -R '^analyze$'` (passes, 15.5s), reproduced the skip path (exit 77) and the `CI=1` Linux fail path (exit 1), and confirmed the flags ctest actually passes: `-std=gnu17 -DSCORE -DCAPTURE -DCLOAKING -Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror -DDEBUG -I/usr/include`.

Nothing here is wrong about the game's behavior; the findings are all in the new script and the claims around it. Three of them are should-fix, and the first one defeats the change's own purpose on the one platform the author says CI will settle.

### Review coverage

Satisfied, and I checked it against the diff rather than taking it. The only player-reachable line is `setup.c:670`, and `ui-review`'s stated coverage — 96 A/B games byte-identical against a `main` build, 35 of them showing a `C` on a scan, 123 instrumented promotions with 0 mismatches — is aimed exactly at that line rather than at journeys the change cannot reach. The edits made after that round were comment-only (`setup.c` has no other change), so per step 6 no rerun was owed. The `CMakeLists.txt` change registers a test and touches no feature flag, so it does not change what is compiled into the game and owes nothing here.

I verified the equivalence independently: inside `if (quadnum >= 100)`, `klhere = quadnum/100 >= 1`, the Klingon loop therefore ran at least once, and `kx[klhere]`/`ky[klhere]` hold the last `dropin`'s `ix`/`iy`. `klhere <= 9` (the block returns for `quadnum > 999`), well inside `kx[21]`/`ky[21]` (`sst.h:272-273`). No `Rand()` calls added or removed, which is why the A/B recordings can be byte-identical.

### Findings

**should-fix — `tests/analyze.sh:51`: bare `mktemp -d`, unchecked, makes the whole test a silent no-op on macOS.**
BSD `mktemp` (macOS) requires a template in the non-`-t` form; `mktemp -d` alone prints usage and exits 1. With no `set -e` and no status check, `work` becomes empty, `set -u` is satisfied, and every subsequent path is absolute: the probe writes `/probe.c`, fails for every candidate, and the script exits 77. ctest reports `Skipped` and the macOS job goes green — indistinguishable from the intended "clang-only machine skips", and precisely the #147 failure mode (a check that never ran, reported as fine) reproduced in the fix for it. It also makes the Homebrew-`gcc-N` question you want CI to answer unanswerable, because macOS will skip for an unrelated reason. `tests/tui.sh:104` already uses the portable form; suggest `work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/sst-analyze.XXXXXX") || exit 1` plus `[ -n "$work" ] || exit 1`. (I could not test on macOS; the consistency argument stands either way, and the unchecked status is a defect regardless of who is right about BSD `mktemp`.)

**should-fix — `tests/analyze.sh:52`: the signal traps do not exit, so the script resumes with its work directory deleted.**
Proved locally under `/bin/sh` (dash): a `trap 'rm -rf "$w"' TERM` handler runs and execution *continues*, after which the EXIT trap fires a second time. Here that means a Ctrl-C during `ctest -R analyze` removes `$work` and then the loop keeps compiling into a directory that no longer exists, printing `FAIL: <file>.c did not analyse clean` with a cascade of gcc errors for all 13 sources and exiting 1 — a fabricated analysis failure from an interrupt. `tests/tui.sh:111-124` documents this exact hazard and uses one trap per signal with an explicit `exit`; match it (`trap 'rm -rf "$work"; exit 130' INT`, `143` TERM, `129` HUP, `141` PIPE).

**should-fix — `tests/analyze.sh:97-102` and `CMakeLists.txt:144-147`: a compiler that passes the probe but fails the canary is fatal, with no fallback, and the macOS comment names only two of three outcomes.**
The probe loop tries `gcc` first, and on macOS `gcc` is Apple clang. If clang ever accepts and ignores `-fanalyzer` (today it errors, which is what makes the probe work), the loop stops there, the canary fails, and the test exits 1 — even though `gcc-15`/`gcc-14` were the next two candidates. Moving the canary compile inside the probe loop turns that into "this candidate cannot analyse, try the next", which is what the loop is for, and costs one extra compile per candidate.

On the deliberate macOS call you asked about: letting CI settle it is defensible, but "Either outcome is fine -- more coverage, or a skip" is the part I'd dispute. GitHub's `macos-latest` images ship Homebrew GCC on `PATH`, so the probe will find `gcc-15`/`gcc-14` rather than skip, and the third outcome is the likely one: Homebrew GCC compiling 13 sources against the macOS SDK under `-Wall -Wextra -Wmissing-prototypes -Werror`, where a single GCC-on-Darwin-only warning (or an SDK header incompatibility after an Xcode bump) turns both macOS jobs red on a check whose analysis value Linux already delivered. Per AGENTS.md's rule that a comment stating what can and cannot happen is read as specification, either say the third outcome exists and that you will treat it by restricting the probe, or restrict it now (e.g. skip on `Darwin` unless an opt-in env var is set).

**nit — `tests/analyze.sh:58`: the hard-coded `gcc-15 gcc-14 gcc-13` list ages into a silent skip.**
On the day the only Homebrew GCC is `gcc-16`, macOS quietly reports `Skipped` again with nobody notified — the same invisible-non-execution shape as above. Consider probing `gcc-*` from `PATH`, or at least noting in the comment that the list needs bumping.

**nit — `tests/analyze.sh:104`, `CMakeLists.txt` comment, `verifier.md:32`: "every .c the build compiles" / "every source" is not true.**
The build also compiles `tests/test_tuifmt.c` and `tests/test_rules.c` (`CMakeLists.txt:51,57`), which this loop does not reach. Given AGENTS.md's insistence that a comment's claim carry its source and hold at its own location, say "every .c in the source root — the 13 the `sst` target links" instead.

**nit — `tests/analyze.sh:42-44` vs `CMakeLists.txt:11-16`: the unconditional `-Werror` quietly overrides the `SST_WERROR` policy.**
`CMakeLists.txt` states the policy that a contributor on an untried compiler "gets the warning and a working build"; after this change they get a working build and a failing `analyze` test from an ordinary `-Wall` warning, since `-Werror` is added whatever the preset says. The rationale for `-Werror` over grepping for `-Wanalyzer` (lines 108-114) is sound and I would not change the mechanism — but one sentence in the CMake comment acknowledging that `ctest --preset debug` is now warning-fatal for this one test would keep the two policy statements from contradicting each other.

**nit — `CMakeLists.txt:157`: `analyze_flags` omits `CMAKE_C_FLAGS_<CONFIG>`.**
The ci-release run therefore analyses unoptimised code and differs from the ci-debug run only by `-DDEBUG`. That is probably the right trade (`-O3` makes `-fanalyzer` slower and noisier, and there are no `assert`s in the tree to care about `-DNDEBUG`), but the comment's "the build's own flags" reads as if optimisation came along, and AGENTS.md specifically notes that some warnings need optimisation to appear. Worth one clause saying `-O`/`-g` are deliberately left out.

**nit — `README.md:147-149`: "without it that one test reports as skipped" is now one of two skippable tests.**
A macOS reader with no Homebrew GCC will see a second `Skipped` and have nothing to look it up against.

**nit — `setup.c:667-669`: "the decrement between them is inside it" reads as a contradiction.**
There is no decrement between `klhere = quadnum/100` and `if (quadnum >= 100)`; the decrement is after the test, inside the block. The intended reading (nothing between them changes `quadnum`) is right, but a reader has to reconstruct it. Something like "nothing between them touches `quadnum` — the only decrement is inside this block" says it in one pass. The rest of the comment checks out.

**nit — `.claude/agents/verifier.md:29-44`: the step does not say what a `Skipped` `analyze` means.**
Output item 4 covers it generically ("never report a skipped check as a pass"), but this is the step whose entire history is a leg that silently did not run; one sentence — a skip means no static analysis ran on this machine and is reported as an environment gap — closes it at the place the verifier will be reading.

### Could not review

- macOS behavior of `mktemp -d` with no template, and whether Homebrew GCC compiles this tree against the macOS SDK cleanly: no macOS here, and no clang installed to test the `-fanalyzer` probe against. Findings 1 and 3 are argued from the repository's own idiom and from the runner images rather than from a run.
- The three mutation proofs cited in `tests/analyze.sh:20-27` and the `ui-review`/`verifier` transcripts: I took their described outcomes as reported, checking only that they are consistent with the diff. I did re-run the skip and CI-fail paths myself, which are the two the author says the earlier proofs structurally could not see.

# Handed the build's own flags rather than restating them here, which
# is what CMakeLists.txt passes and why. -Werror is added whatever the
# preset says: this test is fatal on a diagnostic even where the build
# it was configured from is not.
flags="${1:-}"
if [ -z "$flags" ]; then
	echo "usage: analyze.sh \"<compile flags>\"" >&2
	exit 2
fi

work=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT HUP INT TERM PIPE

# Find a compiler whose -fanalyzer is real. Asking the version string is
# not enough: macOS ships clang as `gcc`, which takes -fanalyzer only as
# far as an error. Compiling something is the question worth asking.
cc=""
for candidate in "${CC:-}" gcc gcc-15 gcc-14 gcc-13; do
	[ -n "$candidate" ] || continue
	command -v "$candidate" >/dev/null 2>&1 || continue
	if echo 'int main(void){return 0;}' > "$work/probe.c" &&
	   "$candidate" -fanalyzer -c -o "$work/probe.o" "$work/probe.c" \
	       >/dev/null 2>&1; then
		cc="$candidate"
		break
	fi
done

if [ -z "$cc" ]; then
	# Linux CI builds with GCC, so a skip there would mean the analyzer
	# had gone missing from the one place it is guaranteed. macOS CI
	# builds with clang and is expected to skip.
	if [ -n "${CI:-}" ] && [ "$(uname -s)" = Linux ]; then
		echo "FAIL: no compiler with -fanalyzer on Linux CI, so nothing was analysed" >&2
		exit 1
	fi
	echo "SKIP: no compiler with a working -fanalyzer" >&2
	exit 77
fi

# Prove the analyzer is live before believing a clean run.
#
# This is here because of how #147 came about. Several passes reported
# `gcc -fanalyzer -fsyntax-only` as clean; -fsyntax-only does not run
# the analyzer at all, so those runs were vacuous and looked exactly
# like a pass. A check that cannot fail is worse than no check, and the
# only way to know this one can is to hand it something broken.
cat > "$work/canary.c" <<'EOF'
#include <stdlib.h>

7. **`.claude/agents/verifier.md:32`** — "`gcc -fanalyzer` over every source" carries the same overclaim you just fixed in `analyze.sh`: it is the thirteen sources the `sst` target links, not `tests/test_tuifmt.c` or `tests/test_rules.c`.

leave uncovered. Worse, nothing says they are: `analyze` prints
`analyze OK` either way, which is the shape of problem #147 was about

By `verifier` on the #147 branch, while checking that the new test
could fail. Filed rather than fixed there: #147 is about the leg
existing at all, and this is about how far it reaches.

Nothing here is cheap, which is why it is its own issue.

- `--param analyzer-max-enodes-per-program-point=` and its siblings
  raise the ceilings, at a cost in run time that wants measuring
  against the 16s the test takes now.

# Verdict: request changes

One should-fix (a stale comment introduced by the round-2 Darwin fix — which is what you asked me to look for), plus four nits and one informational finding. Everything else I checked held up, including the two things you flagged for scrutiny.

**State reviewed:** HEAD `1ff91fe` (= `main`, no commits on the branch); unstaged modifications to `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/setup.c`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `README.md`, `.claude/agents/verifier.md`; untracked `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/analyze.sh`. Nothing staged.

## What I verified independently

- **`setup.c` is behavior-identical.** `quadnum` is a local (`setup.c:582`), `klhere = quadnum/100` at 618, the gate at 647, and the only two decrements at 649 and 695 — both after the gate, nothing between 618 and 647 touching it. So `klhere >= 1` inside the block, the drop-in loop ran, and `kx[klhere]/ky[klhere]` is the square `ix/iy` held. `kx[21]`, `klhere <= 9`, so no bound risk. `sortkl()` runs after, so pre-sort indexing matches the super-commander branch's existing `kx[1]` idiom. `ctest --preset ci-debug -R '^golden$'` passes byte-for-byte after rebuild.
- **The comment claims about the diagnostic hold.** HEAD's `setup.c` under `gcc -fanalyzer` gives `-Wanalyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value` at `setup.c:662`; plain `-Wall -Wextra -O3` with no analyzer gives nothing. So "the plain warning set does not see it" is right, and the false positive is real (the read is safe).
- **The coverage table reproduces.** I planted the same shape of uninitialized read (loop-set index over `klhere`) in five functions on a copy outside the repo and compiled with the flags CMake passes: `newqad()` caught, `phasers()` caught, `cloak()` missed, `cramen()` missed, `tui_shutdown()` missed. Your table is accurate, and the per-function conclusion is real — `battle.c` genuinely catches one and misses another.
- **The Darwin gate behaves as described.** With a faked `uname`: Darwin + `CC` unset → SKIP 77; Darwin + `CC=clang` → SKIP 77; Darwin + `CC` unset + `CI=1` → SKIP 77 (correct, macOS CI is expected to skip); Darwin + `CC=gcc` → analyses. CI sets no `CC` on either runner, so Linux CI reaches `/usr/bin/cc` via `$buildcc`.
- **Plumbing.** The `$<TARGET_PROPERTY:sst,SOURCES>` generator expression lands as one semicolon-joined argument in all three `CTestTestfile.cmake`s. `analyze` runs in 14.8 s against a 180 s timeout. 12/12 tests registered. `shellcheck -s sh` clean. Script is `+x`.

## Findings

### Should-fix

**`CMakeLists.txt:173-178`** — the "compiler comes from the build" paragraph is no longer true on Darwin, and the example it gives is a Darwin one.

> The compiler and the source list come from the build too… a tree configured with a different CMAKE_C_COMPILER would otherwise be analysed by whatever gcc the script found… The canary still decides whether the compiler named here can analyse at all, so an AppleClang still skips.

After the round-2 fix, `tests/analyze.sh:123` sets `candidates="${CC:-}"` on Darwin, which drops `$buildcc` entirely. So on macOS the compiler does *not* come from the build: a tree configured with `-DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc-14` and no `CC` skips, and an AppleClang skips because the gate never offers it to the canary, not because the canary rejected it. Failure scenario: a maintainer reading this believes the canary is what keeps AppleClang out and removes or loosens the Darwin gate as redundant; or a macOS contributor who deliberately configured the whole build with GCC gets a silent skip and no clue why. Fix: add the exception — e.g. "…except on Darwin, where only `CC` is consulted and the build's own compiler is not tried" — and, if you want the two paragraphs to agree, `candidates="${CC:-} $buildcc"` on Darwin, which costs macOS CI nothing (AppleClang fails the canary) and cannot introduce SDK-under-`-Werror` risk that the configured build does not already carry.

### Nits

**`tests/analyze.sh:32-33`** — "battle.c catches one and, measured separately, misses another" does not name the function, and #171's comment attributes that data point to "the original report" rather than to a measurement. The claim is true (I confirmed it is `cloak()`), but as written the next reader cannot check the load-bearing sentence in a minute, and the wording is stronger than the source you cite for it. Fix: name `cloak()`, and say whether it was re-measured or carried over.

**`.claude/agents/verifier.md:41`** — ` -- ` in prose where this file uses `—` nine times and `code-review.md`/`ui-review.md` use `--` in prose zero times. Before this diff `verifier.md` had no prose `--` at all; now it has exactly one line with it. Fix: use em dashes there for the file's own convention (the `--` convention is for C comments and shell scripts, which is where `analyze.sh` and `CMakeLists.txt` correctly use it).

**`.claude/agents/verifier.md:46-48`** — telling the verifier that a SKIPPED `analyze` is "an environment gap to report as one" conflicts with `CMakeLists.txt:144-147`, where the macOS skip is by design. A verifier on a macOS dev machine will report a deliberate decision as a gap on every pass, which is how a real gap gets tuned out. Fix: distinguish — a skip on Linux (or anywhere GCC is the build compiler) is a gap; on Darwin without `CC` it is the documented default.

**`CMakeLists.txt:158-159`** — "The cost is a contributor on a newer GCC seeing `analyze` go red over code they did not touch" understates the cost by naming only the contributor. `ubuntu-latest` bumping its default GCC lands the same red on CI for every PR and on `main`, with no local change to blame it on. Fix: say so, and say what the intended response is (fix, or annotate the site).

### Informational — worth a comment on #171, not a change here

The "too complex" mechanism is real and I identified the parameter: all three misses are recovered by `--param analyzer-bb-explosion-factor=40` (default 5), with no `-Wanalyzer-too-complex` diagnostic emitted at either setting.

```
battle.c cloak()      default 0 -> bb-factor=40: caught
sst.c    cramen()     default 0 -> bb-factor=40: caught
tui.c    tui_shutdown default 0 -> bb-factor=40: caught
```

That confirms the sentence at `tests/analyze.sh:27-28` and at `verifier.md:49-50` (gcc gives up silently), and it corrects #171's own comment, which concluded that what decides this is unknown and named `analyzer-max-enodes-per-program-point` as the guess — that param alone changes nothing here; `analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` is the binding one. I would *not* raise it in the test: deeper analysis means more false positives of exactly the `newqad()` kind, on a check that is `-Werror`. Per AGENTS.md step 9 this belongs as a comment on #171, filed by you.

## Review coverage

Your `ui-review` skip is justified and I am not disputing it. The `setup.c` edit is provably the same square and the `golden` recordings pass byte-for-byte after a rebuild, which is independent evidence rather than reasoning; the `CMakeLists.txt` addition introduces `analyze_flags` as a new variable and does not touch `CMAKE_C_FLAGS` or the `sst` target, so nothing about what is compiled into the game changes — the condition in "The review sub-agents" that makes a build-system change reach the player is not met. `README.md`, `verifier.md` and `tests/analyze.sh` are not player-facing. You told me which passes ran and that the last `ui-review` round predates only non-player-facing changes; that matches the diff.

## Not reviewed

- macOS behavior beyond the faked-`uname` simulation — I have no Darwin machine, so the Homebrew-`gcc-N`-on-path scenario is reasoned from the code path, not observed.
- The full `ctest --preset ci-release` run; I ran `analyze` and `golden` under `ci-debug` only, and took your 12/12 report for the rest. That is the `verifier`'s scope.
- Whether a future `ubuntu-latest` GCC emits new analyzer diagnostics on this tree — untestable here; GCC 15.2.0 locally is clean.

# Verdict: request changes

One should-fix (a stale comment introduced by the round-2 Darwin fix — which is what you asked me to look for), plus four nits and one informational finding. Everything else I checked held up, including the two things you flagged for scrutiny.

**State reviewed:** HEAD `1ff91fe` (= `main`, no commits on the branch); unstaged modifications to `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/setup.c`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `README.md`, `.claude/agents/verifier.md`; untracked `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/tests/analyze.sh`. Nothing staged.

## What I verified independently

- **`setup.c` is behavior-identical.** `quadnum` is a local (`setup.c:582`), `klhere = quadnum/100` at 618, the gate at 647, and the only two decrements at 649 and 695 — both after the gate, nothing between 618 and 647 touching it. So `klhere >= 1` inside the block, the drop-in loop ran, and `kx[klhere]/ky[klhere]` is the square `ix/iy` held. `kx[21]`, `klhere <= 9`, so no bound risk. `sortkl()` runs after, so pre-sort indexing matches the super-commander branch's existing `kx[1]` idiom. `ctest --preset ci-debug -R '^golden$'` passes byte-for-byte after rebuild.
- **The comment claims about the diagnostic hold.** HEAD's `setup.c` under `gcc -fanalyzer` gives `-Wanalyzer-use-of-uninitialized-value` at `setup.c:662`; plain `-Wall -Wextra -O3` with no analyzer gives nothing. So "the plain warning set does not see it" is right, and the false positive is real (the read is safe).
- **The coverage table reproduces.** I planted the same shape of uninitialized read (loop-set index over `klhere`) in five functions on a copy outside the repo and compiled with the flags CMake passes: `newqad()` caught, `phasers()` caught, `cloak()` missed, `cramen()` missed, `tui_shutdown()` missed. Your table is accurate, and the per-function conclusion is real — `battle.c` genuinely catches one and misses another.
- **The Darwin gate behaves as described.** With a faked `uname`: Darwin + `CC` unset → SKIP 77; Darwin + `CC=clang` → SKIP 77; Darwin + `CC` unset + `CI=1` → SKIP 77 (correct, macOS CI is expected to skip); Darwin + `CC=gcc` → analyses. CI sets no `CC` on either runner, so Linux CI reaches `/usr/bin/cc` via `$buildcc`.
- **Plumbing.** The `$<TARGET_PROPERTY:sst,SOURCES>` generator expression lands as one semicolon-joined argument in all three `CTestTestfile.cmake`s. `analyze` runs in 14.8 s against a 180 s timeout. 12/12 tests registered. `shellcheck -s sh` clean. Script is `+x`.

## Findings

### Should-fix

**`CMakeLists.txt:173-178`** — the "compiler comes from the build" paragraph is no longer true on Darwin, and the example it gives is a Darwin one.

> The compiler and the source list come from the build too… a tree configured with a different CMAKE_C_COMPILER would otherwise be analysed by whatever gcc the script found… The canary still decides whether the compiler named here can analyse at all, so an AppleClang still skips.

After the round-2 fix, `tests/analyze.sh:123` sets `candidates="${CC:-}"` on Darwin, which drops `$buildcc` entirely. So on macOS the compiler does *not* come from the build: a tree configured with `-DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc-14` and no `CC` skips, and an AppleClang skips because the gate never offers it to the canary, not because the canary rejected it. Failure scenario: a maintainer reading this believes the canary is what keeps AppleClang out and removes or loosens the Darwin gate as redundant; or a macOS contributor who deliberately configured the whole build with GCC gets a silent skip and no clue why. Fix: add the exception — e.g. "…except on Darwin, where only `CC` is consulted and the build's own compiler is not tried" — and, if you want the two paragraphs to agree, `candidates="${CC:-} $buildcc"` on Darwin, which costs macOS CI nothing (AppleClang fails the canary) and cannot introduce SDK-under-`-Werror` risk that the configured build does not already carry.

### Nits

**`tests/analyze.sh:32-33`** — "battle.c catches one and, measured separately, misses another" does not name the function, and #171's comment attributes that data point to "the original report" rather than to a measurement. The claim is true (I confirmed it is `cloak()`), but as written the next reader cannot check the load-bearing sentence in a minute, and the wording is stronger than the source you cite for it. Fix: name `cloak()`, and say whether it was re-measured or carried over.

**`.claude/agents/verifier.md:41`** — ` -- ` in prose where this file uses `—` nine times and `code-review.md`/`ui-review.md` use `--` in prose zero times. Before this diff `verifier.md` had no prose `--` at all; now it has exactly one line with it. Fix: use em dashes there for the file's own convention (the `--` convention is for C comments and shell scripts, which is where `analyze.sh` and `CMakeLists.txt` correctly use it).

**`.claude/agents/verifier.md:46-48`** — telling the verifier that a SKIPPED `analyze` is "an environment gap to report as one" conflicts with `CMakeLists.txt:144-147`, where the macOS skip is by design. A verifier on a macOS dev machine will report a deliberate decision as a gap on every pass, which is how a real gap gets tuned out. Fix: distinguish — a skip on Linux (or anywhere GCC is the build compiler) is a gap; on Darwin without `CC` it is the documented default.

**`CMakeLists.txt:158-159`** — "The cost is a contributor on a newer GCC seeing `analyze` go red over code they did not touch" understates the cost by naming only the contributor. `ubuntu-latest` bumping its default GCC lands the same red on CI for every PR and on `main`, with no local change to blame it on. Fix: say so, and say what the intended response is (fix, or annotate the site).

### Informational — worth a comment on #171, not a change here

The "too complex" mechanism is real and I identified the parameter: all three misses are recovered by `--param analyzer-bb-explosion-factor=40` (default 5), with no `-Wanalyzer-too-complex` diagnostic emitted at either setting.

```
battle.c cloak()      default 0 -> bb-factor=40: caught
sst.c    cramen()     default 0 -> bb-factor=40: caught
tui.c    tui_shutdown default 0 -> bb-factor=40: caught
```

That confirms the sentence at `tests/analyze.sh:27-28` and at `verifier.md:49-50` (gcc gives up silently), and it corrects #171's own comment, which concluded that what decides this is unknown and named `analyzer-max-enodes-per-program-point` as the guess — that param alone changes nothing here; `analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` is the binding one. I would *not* raise it in the test: deeper analysis means more false positives of exactly the `newqad()` kind, on a check that is `-Werror`. Per AGENTS.md step 9 this belongs as a comment on #171, filed by you.

## Review coverage

Your `ui-review` skip is justified and I am not disputing it. The `setup.c` edit is provably the same square and the `golden` recordings pass byte-for-byte after a rebuild, which is independent evidence rather than reasoning; the `CMakeLists.txt` addition introduces `analyze_flags` as a new variable and does not touch `CMAKE_C_FLAGS` or the `sst` target, so nothing about what is compiled into the game changes — the condition in "The review sub-agents" that makes a build-system change reach the player is not met. `README.md`, `verifier.md` and `tests/analyze.sh` are not player-facing. You told me which passes ran and that the last `ui-review` round predates only non-player-facing changes; that matches the diff.

## Not reviewed

- macOS behavior beyond the faked-`uname` simulation — I have no Darwin machine, so the Homebrew-`gcc-N`-on-path scenario is reasoned from the code path, not observed.
- The full `ctest --preset ci-release` run; I ran `analyze` and `golden` under `ci-debug` only, and took your 12/12 report for the rest. That is the `verifier`'s scope.
- Whether a future `ubuntu-latest` GCC emits new analyzer diagnostics on this tree — untestable here; GCC 15.2.0 locally is clean.

content.text:
All four CI jobs pass, and the logs settle both open questions: **`analyze` Passed on both ubuntu legs** (5.4s — so ubuntu's gcc, which isn't the one this was developed against, analyses the tree clean) and **Skipped on both macOS legs**, exactly as the Darwin gate intends. **[PR #172](https://github.com/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/pull/172)** is ready.

**The gap** — `verifier.md`'s step 2 asked for cppcheck, clang-tidy or scan-build "if installed". None is installed here or in CI, so that leg *never ran anywhere*. Every pass reported the gap honestly and it stayed open. It's now `gcc -fanalyzer` over the game's sources, `-Werror`, as a ctest test that fails rather than skips on Linux CI.

**Two things the work turned up.** `gcc -fanalyzer -fsyntax-only` analyses nothing — it exits 0 on a blatant use-after-free — and several verifier passes this session had reported it as a clean substitute. Those weren't weaker checks; they were no check, reported as clean. So the script now picks its compiler by compiling a deliberate use-after-free. And cppcheck couldn't be verified here at all (no root, and the extracted package won't start), so choosing it would have meant shipping a check nobody here could execute — the same shape of gap.

**Review found seven things I didn't**, two of which are the same failure mode as the issue itself: `SKIP_RETURN_CODE 77` was missing, so the skip path was a *failure* — and all three of my mutation proofs ran the script directly and structurally couldn't see it. Then bare `mktemp -d` fails on macOS, which would have left `$work` empty, the probe unable to write, and a green macOS job with nothing analysed — #147's own hole rebuilt inside the fix for it.

**My own measurement was wrong once**, and finding out why mattered: I reported `analyzer-bb-explosion-factor` didn't recover `cloak()`. Two passes disagreed. My probe harness ran `git checkout` after each compile, so every value after the first tested the restored file — a loop returning the same answer for every input should have told me.

**Filed as #171**: the check's reach is per *function*, not per file — caught in `newqad()` and `phasers()`, missed in `cramen()`, `tui_shutdown()` and `cloak()` — and `-Wanalyzer-too-complex` never fires, so the give-up is silent. Thresholds and timings are measured in the script's comment.

Merge it?
